title: From doing to directing

content_blocks.text: When AI hands you something mediocre, the prompt is usually the reason it landed flat, and the prompt is also where you fix it.

Most people who come away unimpressed with AI wrote a vague request and got a vague answer back. The model did its job. It filled the gaps you left, and it filled them with the most generic plausible thing it could reach for. Prompting is a skill, and unlike most skills it improves in minutes, not months. The payoff is immediate, and a sharper instruction turns a throwaway draft into something you can forward, edit lightly, or actually decide from.

This lesson covers the four things that make a prompt good in the first place: specificity, audience, format, and constraints. Whether you are prepping talking points for a vendor negotiation or just trying to get a usable draft of an awkward email, the same four decisions do most of the work. Get them right and most of your frustration disappears.
Specificity: say what you actually want

The most common mistake is asking for too little. "Summarise this document" is a prompt, but it forces the model to guess how long, for whom, and to what end. Now compare that against a fuller version. "Summarise this vendor contract in five bullet points for a non-technical colleague, focusing only on the clauses that carry a cost or a deadline." The second gets you something usable on the first pass. The first gets you a coin flip.

Every guess you leave in a prompt is a decision you have handed to the model, and it will make that decision generically, with no idea what you had in mind. Cutting those guesses is all that specificity means. The extra words are just what it takes to get there.
Vague in, vague out. If the output feels generic, look at your prompt before you blame the model. You almost certainly left the important choices unspecified.
The four levers
For anything you intend to use directly, four decisions carry most of the weight. You will not need all four every time, but naming them takes ten seconds and saves you a round trip.

cards.body: Who is this for? Notes for your own prep read nothing like a message you send to the vendor. State it: for my own use, for a colleague who was not in the room, for a new hire. The model calibrates vocabulary, depth, and what it assumes they already know.
cards.title: Audience

cards.body: What should the output look like? Bullet points, three short paragraphs, a table with named columns, a one-line answer. If you have a shape in mind and do not say so, you get whatever the model defaults to.
cards.title: Format

cards.body: What stance should it take? Neutral analysis, a clear recommendation, or a list of risks only. Asking the model to frame a problem is a different request from asking it to solve one. Decide which you want.
cards.title: Angle

cards.body: What are the hard limits? A word cap, a tone to hold, jargon to avoid. Constraints keep the output inside the box you need it to fit.
cards.title: Constraints

content_blocks.text: Take a real case. You are preparing talking points for a contract renewal with a software vendor who has just proposed a double-digit price increase. "Help me prepare for this negotiation" leaves everything open. Instead: "Draft talking points for our renewal call. We have used this vendor for three years and rely on it daily. They want a large annual increase, and I want to hold it near inflation and add two user seats. Give me three opening positions and the likely pushback on each. Direct, businesslike tone, no filler, one page." Audience, format, angle, and constraints, all decided by you rather than left to the model.
Constraints work in the negative, too

Telling the model what to avoid is as powerful as telling it what to do, and most people never do it. If the output keeps coming back with the same flaw, name the flaw.

The patterns that come up most: "Do not open with a preamble. Start with the first point." "Do not suggest fixes; I only want the problem framed." "Do not use corporate filler like leverage, synergy, or holistic." "Do not exceed 200 words." None of these is a nitpick. A recurring annoyance you keep editing out by hand is a one-line instruction you have not written yet.
If you find yourself deleting the same thing from every output, stop deleting and start excluding. Name it in the prompt.
Anatomy of a strong prompt

The difference is intention, not creativity. Watch what happens when the four levers meet a weak request.

**Weak:** "Write talking points for my vendor call."

**Strong:** "Write talking points for a 30-minute renewal call with our IT vendor. Open with the value we have had from them, then make the case that their proposed increase runs above market, and close with the two concessions I need to walk away satisfied. Firm but friendly tone, under 250 words, no header."

The strong version came from decisions made up front rather than a better imagination. It said who it is for, what shape it takes, what it should do, and what it must not do. That is all it comes down to.
A note on where this goes next

You can push quality further with heavier techniques, such as showing the model a worked example of what good looks like, or giving it a role to shift its perspective, like asking it to pressure-test your talking points the way the vendor account manager would. Those are genuine multipliers, and they get their own lesson. For now, the four levers plus a clear statement of what to avoid will handle most of your work. Master the baseline before reaching for the extras.
The habit worth building

Before you send a prompt for anything that matters, run a two-second check: have I said who it is for, what it should look like, what stance to take, and what to avoid? You will skip some of those on purpose, and that is fine. The point is that you decided, instead of leaving the model to guess. That habit separates the people who find AI useful from the people who find it disappointing.

title: How to write a good prompt

content_blocks.text: Take the folder of raw meeting notes sitting in your week, the ones that still need turning into decisions, owners, and next steps. This lesson runs that one task from start to finish.

Everything so far has built toward a single ability: taking work you actually own, putting an AI tool to it, and keeping enough judgement in the loop to trust what comes out. Here you do it on something real. The task you pick should be one you would have had to do this week anyway, not a demo.
Choose the right task to start with

The best first task is one you do often, that eats real time, and where you can tell good output from bad because you know the subject. That last point matters most. If you cannot judge the result, you cannot catch what AI gets wrong, and this lesson is as much about building your eye as about saving time.

Skip anything that touches a hard no-go zone. Final decisions that carry legal or personal weight, confidential material that cannot go into your tool, work where a plausible-but-wrong answer would slip through unnoticed. You already hold those judgements. Apply them before you start, not after.

One task fits almost any role and makes a good first run: turning a pile of messy meeting notes into a clean list of decisions, owners, and open questions. Whatever you choose, it should be real work with a deadline you already have.
Run it through, step by step
Set up the prompt

Start with the four things every prompt needs: the task, the audience, the format you want, and any constraints. If you have a strong example of what good looks like, paste it in; a model matches a shown standard far better than a described one. Give it the source material it needs and nothing it should not have.

For your meeting notes, hand over the raw text and tell the model to keep firm decisions separate from open questions rather than blur the two, and to attach an owner to every action it can find one for.
Read the first output like an editor, not a reader

The first pass is a draft. Read it the way you would scrutinise a colleague's proposal before it goes up, hunting for gaps, weak claims, and lines that sound right but are not. Check anything factual against the source. A figure, a name, or a date the model produced on its own is exactly where a hallucination hides. If the task list names a deadline or an owner that appears nowhere in the notes, that is your signal to check before you send it on.
Refine, do not restart

Most first drafts land close but wrong in a specific way. Too long, the wrong emphasis, a section that missed the point. Name the fix and ask again, and keep the thread going while it is still improving. Start fresh only when the output has drifted so far that correcting it costs more than a clean prompt would. Knowing which situation you are in is the instinct you have been building all along.

cards.body: Each turn gets closer. Your corrections land, and the model holds the context and builds on it. When that is happening, keep steering from inside the same conversation.
cards.title: Stay in the thread

cards.body: Corrections stop sticking, the output contradicts an earlier turn, or you are spending more effort patching than a clean prompt would take. When that is the pattern, reset with a sharper opening prompt.

content_blocks.text: Close the loop: you own what leaves your hands

When the output is good enough, it is still yours. Do the final read as the person accountable for it, because you are. Confirm the facts hold, the tone fits the audience, and nothing confidential slipped in along the way. Then send it, file it, or carry it into the meeting as your own work.
This goes out under your name. Verification is the step that makes the speed safe to rely on, and skipping it means standing behind a draft you never actually checked.

Do this once with a real task and something shifts. The abstract advice from earlier modules turns into a workflow you can feel. You see where AI saved you an hour, where your judgement was the thing that mattered, and where you would push harder next time. That felt sense is worth more than any single output. It is what lets you take on the next task with confidence and know exactly what to check.
What you should notice by the end

You moved from doing the task to directing it. You set the frame, supplied the context, judged the drafts, corrected what was off, and verified before anything left your hands. That is the whole track in one pass, and it repeats on the next task, and the one after that.

title: Work through a real recurring task with AI

content_blocks.text: A model fails in a handful of predictable places. The same weak points turn up again and again, whatever you happen to be working on. Learn where they sit and you can keep working fast and still catch the bad output before it reaches anyone.

Picture the budget you are pulling together ahead of a decision meeting: last quarter's actuals, a couple of forecasts, and a recommendation on where the money should go next. A model can draft most of that in minutes. It can also get four specific things wrong, in ways that survive a quick read and land in the room looking finished. This lesson walks through those four, where the mechanism you have already met, plausible text rather than looked-up fact, does its most reliable damage, and what each one costs you.
Stale information

A model knows what it was trained on, up to a cutoff date, and nothing after it. Ask it about a tax threshold that changed last quarter, a supplier that raised its rates in March, or a regulation amended since its training, and it answers with the same steady confidence it uses for facts that have held for a decade. It has no built-in sense that its knowledge expires.

The cost hides in plain sight, because the answer reads as current. A budget built on last year's rates. A pricing recommendation resting on market conditions that have since moved. A cost line that misses a supplier increase half the room already knows about. Each one reads perfectly, and each is quietly out of date. Unless the tool is pulling live data, treat anything time-sensitive as a draft you still have to date-check.
Weak arithmetic and quantitative reasoning

On its own, a model writes the text of a calculation. It does not run the calculation. It generates the digits that most plausibly follow the words "the total is", which is a different act from adding the numbers up. Some tools now run real code and compute exactly, and where that happens the maths is genuine. Until you know a real calculation ran, treat every figure as text shaped like a number.

It often lands close, and close is the dangerous part: a total that is off by a little slips past the review a wildly absurd number never would. This bites hardest in the very work you would most want to hand off. Summing the columns in a budget, working out a percentage change on a forecast, or reconciling two totals that should agree are the moments the model looks most useful and is least reliable. Multi-step reasoning breaks the same way. Each step reads as sound, the chain compounds one small slip, and the conclusion arrives confident and wrong.

The more a task turns on numbers or a chain of logical steps, the less its answer is worth at face value. And the more it looks like the model just saved you the effort, the more of that effort has simply moved to checking it.
Bias

A model learned from an enormous body of human writing, and it absorbed the patterns there, including the skewed ones. Ask it to sketch a candidate for a senior role, name a typical customer, or describe who does what on a team, and its defaults track the majority patterns in its training data rather than the people actually in front of you.

This surfaces in two places. In anything that touches people, such as hiring language, performance notes, or assumptions about an audience, the model can dress a stereotype up as professional-sounding prose. And when you ask it to weigh options, it leans toward the conventional, mainstream take, which makes it a poor source of real contrarian challenge. Left unchecked, it narrows your thinking at the exact moment you wanted it widened. If you manage no one, the same caution holds for your own work. The vendor shortlist it drafts or the survey comments it summarises inherit its defaults, not your read of the situation.
Reasoning gaps

The model is fluent, and fluency reads as competence. It does not reliably hold a complex argument together. It will miss the load-bearing assumption in a proposal, accept a flawed premise you hand it, or contradict something it claimed three paragraphs earlier, none of it flagged.

The sharper risk is agreeableness. Push back on its answer and it will often fold and reverse, whether or not you had a point. Frame a question so it implies the answer you are hoping for and it tends to hand that answer straight back. So when you ask it to stress-test the case for a budget before the meeting, it makes a weak challenger: better at producing a first pass than at judging whether that pass holds up. Honest friction is the one thing you most want there, and the one thing it is least able to give.
What this costs, in one line

None of these failures announces itself. Whether the output is right or wrong, it comes back equally fluent, formatted, and confident. The error you spot is cheap; you fix it and move on. The expensive one is the plausible mistake that reads perfectly and gets forwarded: a stale rate in the budget, a total that does not add up in the pricing case, a stereotype in a job description, an assumption nobody challenged sitting under a recommendation. That is how AI usually fails at work. It hands you a confident, well-dressed mistake, and the mistake goes out under your name.

title: What AI consistently gets wrong

content_blocks.text: Where AI earns its keep

AI is strongest when the work is open-ended language and weakest when it turns on facts, figures, or judgment only you can supply. A project post-mortem sits right on that line. The write-up, the timeline, the tidy list of what happened: that is language work, and AI is fast at it. What actually went wrong, and what your team should do differently: that stays with you. Whether you are chairing the review or just accounting for your own part of the project, the split lands the same way.

Think in task categories, not tools. The same model that turns your scattered incident notes into a clean timeline in seconds will also name the wrong root cause with total confidence. What changed between those two results is the kind of task you handed it, not the tool.
The four things it does well
Most of what AI genuinely accelerates falls into four buckets. They share a trait: the value is in producing fluent language or structure, and a human still owns the final call.

cards.body: Open-ended work with words: writing, summarising, reasoning through a problem out loud. Hand it your scattered post-mortem notes and it returns a first-pass timeline with decisions, owners, and open questions. What comes back is a rough document you then shape further.
cards.title: Thinking and drafting

cards.body: Turning information from one form into another: a requirements list into a table, a dense policy clause into plain language, raw notes into a slide outline. Reliable, because the source material sits right in front of it.
cards.title: Structured transformation

cards.body: Emails, summaries, the opening draft of the post-mortem writeup itself. You get something usable in seconds and spend your time refining instead of staring at a blank page.
cards.title: First-draft generation

cards.body: Pulling together what is generally known about a topic into a starting map: a quick primer on how other teams run blameless retros, say, that you then check and sharpen against your own situation.
cards.title: Broad synthesis

content_blocks.text: The pattern across all four: AI is fast at the first 80 percent of language work. The last 20 percent stays with you: the accuracy, the judgment, the sign-off.
The four places it falls short

The limits are just as predictable. They cluster where the task stops being about producing plausible language and starts being about something the model cannot reliably do.

**Calculation and live facts.** On its own, a language model does not calculate. It produces text that looks like a computed answer, and it has no live data unless a tool feeds it some. So when a post-mortem draft says the outage lasted 47 minutes or that response times tripled, treat those as text shaped like numbers until you check them against the actual logs. Both limits lift when the tool is wired for it, since some now run real code or reach a live source. Unless you know that is happening, a duration or a cost it hands you is a claim to verify rather than a figure it worked out.

**Novel judgment with no clear right answer.** Deciding what really caused the slip, and what to change next time, is the part of the post-mortem that matters most. When that call turns on competing accounts of what happened, or on which risk is worth carrying, AI gives you something generic and reasonable-sounding. It cannot make the trade-off for you, because the trade-off depends on what you know and value, not on what plausibly comes next. That holds whether you run the review or simply speak to your own slice of it.

**Anything needing context it does not have.** The model has what you told it and what it absorbed in training. The real reason a project stalled is often the thing nobody wrote down: the deadline that was political, the corner someone was quietly told to cut, the disagreement that never made the minutes. None of that reached the model. Missing context does not stop it from answering. It answers as if the gap were not there.

**High-stakes precision work.** Financial modelling, regulatory decisions, anything carrying legal or safety weight. The task itself demands an exactness the model does not guarantee, so it sits outside what you can hand over and accept as-is.
Across every category, one rule holds: AI output is a starting point a human checks, never a finished product you forward untouched.
Ask whether it needs AI at all

Part of the skill is knowing when not to reach for it. A recurring email wants a saved template. A known process wants a checklist. A single fact wants an ordinary search. Pointing a language model at work that a plain search or a saved template would handle faster and more reliably is its own small mistake. What you are after is the outcome, and often the older tool gets you there sooner.
The instinct to build

Before you hand off a piece of the post-mortem, run one quick test: is this mostly about producing language and structure, or does it turn on a number, a fact, or a judgment about what really happened? The first kind AI does well and fast. The second it will answer anyway, confidently and often wrong. Learning to feel that difference before you delegate is most of what separates the people who get real value from AI from the people who do not.

title: What AI is good at, and where it falls short

content_blocks.text: A colleague hands you a paragraph of dense technical language, a clause on data residency, say, and asks you to make it readable for the whole company. Stripping the jargon is a clean hand-off to a model. Deciding which caveat cannot be simplified away without making the result quietly wrong is not.

You already run this calculation whenever you pass a task to someone else, weighing what it costs to brief and check them against what it costs to just do it yourself. Handing work to AI is the same discipline with one difference. The model is fast and never tires, but it arrives with none of your context, and it carries none of the accountability when the call turns out wrong. If you manage nobody and have never delegated a thing, the same judgment still applies, aimed at your own work: which parts to hand off, and which to keep because only you can do them right.
The two questions that decide it

Before you hand anything off, ask two things.

First, how much task-specific context does this need? Context the model cannot pull from the words in front of it: who is in the room, why a timeline really slipped, which stakeholder is privately opposed. For the plain-language rewrite, the context that matters is narrow. Which regulatory detail is load-bearing and which is decoration, and you can hand that over in a sentence. When a task turns on context you cannot supply that cheaply, either keep it or brief the model properly first. When it needs little, it is a strong candidate to pass on.

Second, what does a subtle error cost, and how easily would you catch one? A mistake that jumps out on a quick read is cheap, because you see it, you fix it, you move on. A mistake only an insider would notice is expensive, because it can pass review and reach a decision-maker intact. In the translation case, a dropped qualifier that changes what the clause actually permits is that kind of quiet, costly error. The harder a mistake is to catch, the more the task belongs with you.

The dangerous combination is high context plus errors that are hard to catch: fluent, confident output that looks right and is wrong in a way only you would spot. That is where the time AI saved comes back to cost you, with interest.
Where the time saving is real

AI pays off on structured, repetitive work, and on moving information from one shape into another. Summarising a long thread. Turning rough notes into a clean table. Rewriting that dense clause in plain words. The quality bar is clear enough for the model to hit, the time saved is genuine, and mistakes tend to surface on review.

Underneath most good delegation sits a split you can make on almost any task: separate the judgment from the assembly. Deciding which findings belong in a report is judgment, so keep it. Writing those findings up once you have chosen them is assembly, so pass it on. Deciding which technical nuance must survive a translation is judgment. Producing the clean plain-language draft around that decision is assembly.

That split is why so much real work is neither fully kept nor fully handed off. You do the thinking; the model does the production.
What to keep

Keep the work whose value lives in the parts a model cannot supply. Novel judgment calls with no obvious right answer and competing risks. Anything that depends on having been in the room. Anything where the output has to reflect your read of the politics, the history, or the people involved.

The model will always give you an answer, and that is the risk. Ask it to recommend a pricing change and it will recommend one, fluently, drawing on nothing about your market, your margins, or your competitors. The answer comes out generic, and your value on that task was the non-generic part. When a task turns on knowing something the model cannot know, holding onto it is exactly where you add value.
A working map

cards.body: Summarising an interview or a long thread. Rewriting a dense clause in plain language. Drafting a standard status update. Writing up findings you have already chosen. Clear quality bar, visible errors, real time saved.

And splitting well depends on doing the judgment part yourself first. Delegate the decision along with the drafting, and the effort you thought you saved is gone. You have handed away the part that was yours to own.

title: What to delegate and what to keep

content_blocks.text: You started this track able to use AI. You finish it able to direct it: knowing what to hand over, what to check, and when to keep your hands on the work.
That shift is what carries. The mechanics of any single tool will change within a year. The judgment you have built will not.
What you now know

Seven things, each building on the last. You know what generative AI really is: a model that predicts text rather than a system that looks up facts. You know enough about how it works to have good instincts, about tokens and context, about why the same prompt gives different answers, about why it can hand you confident nonsense in a fluent voice. You can write a prompt that gets a usable result, supply the context the model cannot see, and work the instruct-review-refine loop instead of taking the first draft as final.

You also know where it fails and what those failures cost: bias, stale information, gaps in reasoning, the tasks that are simply off-limits. You know how to verify before you forward or decide, what should never be pasted into a tool, and that whatever goes out is yours to stand behind. And you have seen the move from doing the work to directing it, choosing what is worth handing off and what needs your own hand. If you manage people, that will feel familiar. If you manage no one, it applies just as squarely to your own work. You are now the one briefing, reviewing, and signing off on things you used to grind out from start to finish.
The core skill is a way of thinking, not a tool. You start from a plain question, what is this task really asking for, then choose the method to fit, including the decision to use no AI at all.
What comes next
The tools you will meet from here sort roughly by the kind of work they support. Learn the categories rather than the products. Products get renamed and replaced; the categories hold.

cards.body: The chat-style tools you already know. Drafting a reply to a customer complaint, turning two hours of messy notes into a task list, putting a technical clause into plain language. Broad, flexible, and the default for most knowledge work.

cards.body: Tools that take several steps on their own and reach into your files, inbox, or systems through connectors. More capable, and more to keep an eye on, because they act rather than only answer.
cards.title: Agentic and connected tools

cards.body: Built for one kind of work: writing code, automating a business process without code, running a personal knowledge base. Deeper inside their lane, weaker outside it.

content_blocks.text: Most tasks land cleanly in one of these. The tool tracks that follow go deep inside each category, into the practical detail of getting real work done with a given product. You already have the foundation they build on. You will judge a new tool by what it does and where it breaks, not by how it is sold.
Where to point it first

Pick one recurring task you already own: the weekly report you always rewrite, the inbox thread that eats an hour, the write-up nobody enjoys drafting. Point AI at that one, check what comes back, and refine your approach over a few real repetitions. Calibration comes from reps on work you can already judge. Experiments on unfamiliar, high-stakes work teach you far less.

title: You're ready: here's what comes next

content_blocks.text: It starts before the model writes

You have your monthly one-on-one with your manager on Thursday, and a month of scattered work to turn into three things worth actually raising. You could open a model and ask for help. What you get back depends less on how you word the request and more on what you put in front of it first.

A good prompt tells the model what to do. Context is the raw material it works with: the project updates you are pulling from, the manager you are writing for, the constraints you already know apply. Get the context right and the difference in output is larger than any clever phrasing. The instinct most people carry over from search, that more input means a better result, works against you here. The model responds to relevance, not volume.
What context actually is

Everything the model can see in one conversation counts as context: your instructions, the files you attach, the data you paste, and the whole back-and-forth up to that point. All of it shapes the answer. So the question that matters is what the task needs.

Think about how you would brief a capable new colleague. You would not drop every document the company owns on their desk and ask for a summary. You would give them the two or three things that matter, tell them who it is for, and flag the one constraint they could not have guessed. The model rewards the same discipline.
What to include
The context worth giving usually comes down to four things. Give the model the ones the task turns on and leave the rest out.

cards.body: The actual thing the task works on: the project updates you are pulling from, the thread you need to reply to, the notes you want turned into actions. Paste the relevant parts and leave the surrounding archive out.
cards.title: The source material

cards.body: Who reads the output and what it is for. A talking-points list for your own one-on-one reads nothing like a summary for the whole team. Say it, because the model cannot guess your reader.
cards.title: The audience and purpose

cards.body: The boundaries the model could not infer: length, tone, what to leave out, a format you must match, a decision already taken. These are what keep a usable draft from going off the rails.
cards.title: The constraints

cards.body: What good looks like. A short example of the tone or structure you want, or one line on what a strong answer covers, sharpens the output more than another paragraph of instruction.
cards.title: The standard to hit

content_blocks.text: Back to Thursday. For your one-on-one, the context that matters is the handful of projects you want to raise, where each one stands, and what you want from your manager on each: a decision, cover for a delay, a heads-up. What does not help is your whole task list for the quarter, every thread the projects touched, or the org chart. That material does not sharpen the talking points. It just gives the model more to wade through before it reaches anything useful.
More is not better

This is the part that cuts against instinct. Overload the context and the model has to reason across all of it to find the few things that matter, and the signal you care about gets diluted by everything sitting around it. The usual culprits are familiar: a 60-page contract pasted whole when the question is about one clause, a raw data export dropped in instead of the relevant rows, a long conversation that began on one thing and wandered through five others.

That last one is easy to miss. In a long, drifting thread, an instruction you gave near the start, keep this under a page, write it for someone non-technical, gets buried under everything that came after and quietly stops being honoured. The model is weighing the whole conversation, and your early steer has become a small voice in a crowded room.
When answers start feeling generic, dropping the constraints you set earlier, or repeating themselves, the context has gone noisy. Clean it up before you reach for a cleverer prompt.

A couple of habits keep it clean. Paste the minimum that does the job: the relevant clause rather than the whole contract, a filtered subset rather than the full export. And where your tool offers a persistent memory or project space, use it for the stable context that rarely shifts, like who the work is for, the format you always use, and the constraints that keep recurring, so you set it once instead of re-explaining it every time. That is what those features are built for: reusable standing context, rather than a store for every document you have ever opened.
What never to include

One rule overrides everything above. Do not paste confidential, personal, or regulated information into an AI tool that has not been approved for it: customer records, employee data, unreleased financials, anything covered by a contract or a regulation. Your one-on-one prep is exactly where this bites. Notes on a colleague's performance problem, a salary figure, something you heard in confidence about a reorg: none of it belongs in an unapproved tool, however much faster it would make the prep. The convenience is real. So is the exposure.
If you would not put it in an email to someone outside the company, do not paste it into an unapproved AI tool. When in doubt, leave it out, or use only a tool that has been approved for it.

This is the short version, enough to keep you out of trouble for now. The full picture on data, approved tools, and where the real risks sit comes later in the track. For here, the rule travels light: relevant beats plentiful, and confidential stays out.

title: Providing context, and what never to include

content_blocks.text: Before a competitive scan lands in the deck for your strategy session, ask the one question that matters: how do you actually know it is right? It reads well and looks complete. Neither of those is evidence.

Verification is a habit you run before output leaves your hands: a short, repeatable check that turns a plausible draft into something you can defend. Take the competitive scan you pull together before a strategy session. The model hands you a tidy page on three rivals, with pricing tiers, headcount, a recent funding round, a couple of product claims. It looks finished. Whether it is right is a separate question, and you are the only one who can answer it.

The reason to bother is ownership. When that scan shapes where the team places its bets, the model does not carry the cost of a wrong number. You do. The same holds if nobody reports to you: the moment you paste a figure into a shared doc or repeat it in a meeting, it becomes your claim, and "the AI said so" is not a defence anyone accepts. Verification is how you turn speed into something you can stand behind.
Match the check to the risk

Not every output needs the same scrutiny. A rough brainstorm you plan to rework barely needs a look. A competitor price that decides how you position your own is worth getting right. Calibrate the effort to two things: how much the task turns on specific facts, and how costly a wrong one would be.
The more an output turns on specific facts, figures, names, or quotes, the more the burden sits with you before you forward it, cite it, or act on it.

A quick reflex helps: ask what happens if this is wrong. If the honest answer is that someone places a bet on bad information or the team loses credibility with the board, the output has bought itself a real check. If the answer is nothing much, move on.
What to check

Verification is not rereading until it feels right. It is checking named claims against a source you trust, one at a time. Fluent prose reads as correct whether or not it is, so a general sense that something seems solid is worth nothing. Check specific things, each tied to a failure mode you already know.

cards.body: Every number, date, name, and quote is a place the model may have produced something plausible and invented. Trace each one back to a source you trust. A competitor funding round stated with full confidence is not proof the round happened.
cards.title: Facts and figures

cards.body: Ask whether the claim depends on recent events or changed circumstances. A model works from training data with a cutoff and does not know what happened after it unless you supplied the material. A rival price or a headcount can be a year out of date.
cards.title: Currency

cards.body: Follow the logic step by step. Output can reach a wrong conclusion through fluent, confident steps that skip a link. Check the chain, not just the answer at the end.
cards.title: Reasoning

cards.body: Ask what is missing, not only whether what is present is true. A scan can be accurate on every line and still leave out the competitor who matters most, or the caveat that would change the decision.
cards.title: Omission and slant

content_blocks.text: Three moves that make checking faster

You do not have to verify everything by hand from a blank slate. A few habits cut the cost.

First, make the claims traceable. When you prompt, ask the model to mark which parts rest on the material you gave it and which come from its own general knowledge. The second kind is where invented detail hides. This does not prove the source-backed claims are right, but it tells you where to look hardest.

Second, check against the source, not against the model. If you handed it a set of analyst notes to condense, verify the summary against those notes. The ground truth is the input you provided, not a second answer from the AI. Asking the model whether it is sure is close to worthless: it will revise a correct answer or defend a wrong one with the same steady confidence.

Third, take anything about the outside world to the outside world. For a market-share figure, a regulation, a rival funding round, confirm it in a real source. Treat the model as a fast way to draft and structure, and go elsewhere for facts about the world. Keeping those two jobs separate is most of the discipline.
Where it goes wrong in practice

The first common failure is checking the wrong thing: polishing tone and flow while the numbers go unexamined. Polish is not accuracy. The second is anchoring. Once you have read a confident, well-formed answer, it is hard to see what is missing, because the draft has already framed the problem for you. Guard against it by deciding what a good answer must contain before you read the model version. For the competitive scan, write down the questions the strategy session has to answer, then check whether each one is genuinely covered and sourced, rather than being led by whatever the model chose to include.
Verification matters most where AI is most convincing: when the output is fluent, complete-looking, and one click from being forwarded.
The workflow in one pass

For any output that carries real weight: decide up front what a good answer must contain; separate the model claims from what your source actually supports; check every fact, figure, and date against a trusted source rather than against the AI; follow the reasoning a step at a time; and ask what has been left out. It takes minutes. Skipping it can cost far more than the minutes it saved.

title: How to verify AI output

content_blocks.text: You do not build good AI instincts by reading about them. You build them by noticing what happened after each round, and why.

You already have the frame: the shift from doing to directing, and the judgement call about what to hand off and what to keep. This lesson is about turning that frame into something faster than reasoning, the point where you stop working it out step by step. A well-calibrated user knows within seconds whether a task is worth handing over, writes a usable brief without labouring over it, and reads the output already knowing what to fix. None of this needs a team. If you turn the same messy meeting notes into a task list most weeks, the calibration happens on your own desk, one round at a time.
What miscalibration looks like
Most people go wrong in a handful of predictable ways. Naming them is the fastest route to catching yourself in the act.

cards.body: You hand over a task without the background it needs. The output comes back polished and confidently wrong in ways that matter. The fix: give the model your context before you ask for output.
cards.title: Over-delegating without context

cards.body: You do a structured, low-stakes task by hand because that is how you have always done it. The fix: when you finish one of these without AI, ask whether that was the right call.

content_blocks.text: How the read gets faster

Calibration is pattern recognition, and every delegation is a data point. Take the notes-to-tasks routine. Did the task list come back usable, or did it invent an owner nobody agreed to and miss the one action that actually mattered? If it missed, ask why: thin context, the wrong task for a model, or a first draft that needed another turn. Over enough rounds you build a mental map of what this kind of work does well and where it slips, and the reasoning collapses into a fast read.

The problem is that most people use AI and move straight on, registering nothing. The output was fine, or it was not, and the moment passes either way. You do not need a log or a system for this. You need the habit of pausing for five seconds after each round to ask what you learned. Calibration costs you almost nothing extra. It is attention, paid to the rounds you are already running.

Repeated disappointment with a task usually means you have not run it enough times to calibrate your brief. It is rarely proof that the task cannot be delegated. Give it enough rounds before you write it off.
Narrow beats broad

Calibrating across everything at once is slow and muddy. Pick one recurring task and use AI for it consistently for two weeks. Your weekly meeting notes are a good candidate: the same shape every time, low stakes, and frequent enough to give you real repetitions.

Watch three things as you go: what it reliably gets right, where it consistently misses, and which adjustments to your brief move the needle most. Narrow focus learns faster and cleaner than attention spread thin. That single repeated task is exactly the kind of work the next module puts into practice, start to finish.

title: Building reliable instincts through use

content_blocks.text: The first output is where the work starts. A short back-and-forth usually gets you further than any single, perfectly crafted prompt.

A lot of weak AI output traces back to one habit: treating each prompt as a single shot. You fire off one instruction, judge whatever comes back, and walk away unimpressed. The more reliable pattern is a loop. Get a draft, work out what is wrong with it, correct that one thing specifically, and go again. Two or three exchanges routinely land somewhere a single prompt never would.

Say a vendor has gone quiet on a deliverable and you ask the model for a follow-up email. This is the same instinct you already use when you hand work to someone else. You would not expect their first draft to be final. You react to it: cut the throat-clearing, lead with the overdue item, soften the closing line. The second version is better because your feedback was concrete. The tool works the same way, only faster. If you manage no one, nothing changes here; you react to the model the way you react to your own rough first attempt at anything.
Reacting is faster than specifying

You could try to anticipate every requirement in one enormous prompt. Usually it is quicker to say roughly what you want, look at what comes back, and redirect from there. Seeing a draft you dislike tells you what you actually want far more precisely than staring at a blank page trying to predict it. One look at a vendor email that reads too aggressively tells you the tone you need better than any adjective you could have supplied up front.
Expect to iterate. A near-miss you can react to is often the quickest route to the version you need.
Make corrections specific

Everything in the loop depends on how you give feedback. Ask the model to make it better and it learns nothing useful; it reshuffles the words and hands you something equally off. Name the actual problem, and name what right looks like.

Compare the two registers. Vague: improve this, make it more professional, not quite right. Specific, on that vendor email: the opening is too soft, so lead with the deliverable and the date it was promised; the second paragraph repeats the first, so cut it; the tone reads irritated, and we want to keep this supplier, so make it firm but neutral. Each of those names what is wrong and what right would look like. That is the difference between a correction that sticks and one that spins the model in circles without moving it forward.
Build long outputs in stages

Not everything is a short email. When you need something substantial, a full vendor evaluation or a multi-section supplier review, do not ask for the finished document in one go. Long outputs drift when you demand everything at once.

Ask for the structure first. An outline is fast to produce and fast to correct, and approving the shape before any real content means a wrong frame gets caught while it is still cheap to change. Then fill it in section by section. Leave tone, word choice, and formatting until the end, once the substance is settled.
Know when to start fresh

Sometimes the loop stops paying off. The model repeats a mistake you have already corrected twice. Each turn drifts further from what you want. Corrections stop sticking. Those are the signals to stop iterating and open a fresh conversation.

Starting fresh consolidates what you have. You take the parts that work, write a cleaner and sharper prompt, and begin again with the accumulated noise stripped out.

cards.body: The history is actively helping. A shared frame is in place, the format is agreed, an output is mid-refinement, or you are asking a direct follow-up. The conversation is carrying useful weight.
cards.title: Keep going when

cards.body: The topic has shifted, quality has drifted over several turns, the model keeps dragging in irrelevant earlier context, or you want an unanchored view that the thread so far has not coloured.
cards.title: Start fresh when

content_blocks.text: The reset has a technique of its own. Do not just retype your prompt into a blank window and lose the good work. Paste the useful draft into the fresh conversation and give sharper instructions around it. You drop what was dragging the thread down and keep the part worth keeping. If your AI tool lets you store stable background, the standing facts about a project or a supplier, starting fresh drops the noise without losing that foundation.
Where this sits

Everything above is the mechanic: instruct, review, refine, and know when to reset. It says nothing yet about the specific moves that make any single turn land harder, things like worked examples, role framing, or asking the model to critique its own draft. Those levers come next.

For now, the loop itself is the skill: expect to iterate, react precisely, build in stages, and reset when the thread stops helping.

title: Working iteratively

content_blocks.text: The quickest way to give back everything AI just saved you is to point it at a task that never belonged with it. Knowing when to stop is a judgment skill, and it belongs to you, not the tool.

So far the track has been about getting more out of the tool: sharper prompts, closer verification, a clear read on where it fails. This lesson is about the opposite discipline, the one that says leave it shut. Some tasks fail the test before verification even comes up, because AI never belonged in them. For those, no prompt and no amount of checking helps. The right move is to not open the tool at all.
The line is about stakes, not difficulty

Difficulty is not the test. A task lands off-limits for one of two reasons: a confident wrong answer would cost more than you can absorb, or using the tool breaks a duty you hold no matter how the answer turns out.

A model produces plausible text. It does not know what is true, and it answers to no one when it gets things wrong. Set those two facts against high stakes and the tool turns into a liability. So the question worth asking before you hand something over is a plain one: if it is confidently wrong here, what happens, and can you live with it?
The hard stops
Some categories stay off the table however convenient AI would be. Treat these as defaults, not suggestions.

cards.body: Anything where a wrong output causes damage you cannot undo: legal filings, medical or safety calls, financial commitments, hiring or firing on the say-so of a model. AI can inform the thinking. It must not make the call.
cards.title: Irreversible or high-harm decisions

cards.body: If the input holds data you are not permitted to share outside the company, the answer quality is beside the point. The only question is whether the tool is allowed to see that input at all. The next lesson covers this in full.
cards.title: Confidential or regulated information you cannot expose

cards.body: If you lack the knowledge, time, or source material to check the output, you cannot use it responsibly. Unverifiable plus consequential is the worst combination. If you cannot check it and it matters, do not ship it.
cards.title: Anything you cannot verify

cards.body: A performance review, a condolence note, a personal recommendation, a hard judgment call your role exists to make. Handing these to a model gives away the very thing your job is there to do, however polished the result comes back.
cards.title: Work that must be genuinely yours

content_blocks.text: The pull of convenience

The dangerous cases are rarely the obvious ones. Nobody sets out to file a fabricated legal citation. It happens because the tool was fast, the output looked right, and the stakes were not felt until later.

Speed is what makes a tool tempting in the very moments it should stay shut. A confident, well-formatted answer to a question you cannot check feels like progress, and under deadline pressure that feeling is the danger. The more a task tempts you to skip the check because you are busy, the more likely it is a task where skipping the check is what hurts you.
The moment you notice you are trusting AI because checking would be inconvenient, stop. That instinct is the signal that you have crossed the line. It is not a licence to cross it anyway.
When it is a judgment call

Most work is not a hard stop. The grey zone is wider, and it is where the real call sits: AI is allowed, but is using it wise?

Take the message announcing a reorg to your team. Nothing forbids you from having a model draft it, and it would hand you something clean and calm in seconds. But the lines that land are the ones that show you understand what people are about to feel, and that read is yours to bring. Let the tool tidy your phrasing once the substance is written. Do not let it decide what the substance is.

The test is ownership. When the message goes out, whose name sits on it, and what are they answerable for? If AI helped with the draft and you still stand fully behind every line because you supplied the judgment, the tool did its job. If you would be using it to stand in for judgment you are the one paid to bring, keep the work yourself, even when nothing formally forbids it.

If you manage no one, the same test still bites. The note where you own a mistake to a customer, or raise a hard worry with your manager, is yours for the same reason: your credibility is what carries it, and no model can supply that.
Keeping it in proportion

None of this argues for caution everywhere. Most day-to-day work carries low stakes and easy checking, and AI belongs there: cleaning up a spreadsheet export, turning a batch of survey comments into themes, drafting the first pass of release notes. The point is narrower. A small set of tasks should never touch the tool, and a slightly larger set earns a deliberate pause before it does. Sorting one from the other is the skill worth building.

title: When not to use AI

content_blocks.text:
When Claude gives you a short answer, it stays in the chat. When it produces something bigger, like a full report or a checklist you plan to reuse, it can open that output in its own panel beside the conversation. That panel is an Artifact. It is not just tidier formatting. It changes what you can do with the output next, because you can edit it, revise it, and copy it out without scrolling back through the chat to find the latest version.

This lesson covers what an Artifact is, when Claude creates one, and how to turn a back-and-forth conversation into a reusable structured output.
What an Artifact is

An Artifact is a separate pane that opens alongside the conversation when Claude produces a substantial piece of content. You read and steer in the chat on one side, and the finished output sits on the other, updating as you refine it.

Claude creates one when the content is substantial enough to work with on its own, rather than for every reply.

cards.body: Reports, process descriptions, templates, communication drafts, checklists. Content you will read as a finished piece rather than a chat message.
cards.title: Documents and structured text

cards.body: Formatted content with headings, tables, and lists. Useful for structured notes or anything destined for a markdown-based tool.
cards.title: Markdown

cards.body: Scripts, queries, formulas, HTML pages, simple visualisations. Some can be previewed live in the pane, so you see the result and not only the code.
cards.title: Code and interactive content

content_blocks.text: For a one-line answer or a quick clarification, Claude just responds in the chat. Artifacts are for outputs long enough to stand alone.
Turning a conversation into a reusable checklist

Suppose you are putting together an onboarding checklist for a new starter on your team. You do not have to write the whole thing up front. Work it out in conversation, then ask Claude to produce the result as an Artifact.

1. **Talk it through first.** Describe the role, the first week, the accounts and access they need, who they should meet. Let Claude ask questions and fill gaps. This is where the thinking happens.
2. **Ask for the output as an Artifact.** Once the content is roughly right, say what you want and what it should look like: "Produce this as a structured onboarding checklist with sections for week one, first month, and access requests, using checkboxes." Being specific about the shape gives Claude more to work with than "write a checklist."
3. **Read it in the pane.** The checklist opens as an Artifact beside the chat. From here you refine it in place rather than regenerating it from scratch.
Ask for what the output should look like, not only what it should contain. Naming the structure, the sections, and the format up front usually saves you an editing round later.
Iterating on the Artifact

Once the Artifact exists, you change it by asking, in the chat, for the specific edit you want. Claude updates the Artifact in place. You might say:

- "Add a section at the end for the 30-day check-in."
- "Turn the access list into a table with the owner for each system."
- "Remove the parts about the office badge, we are fully remote."

If an edit takes the checklist in the wrong direction, Claude keeps a version history on the Artifact, so you can go back to an earlier state rather than trying to undo the change by hand.

Artifacts live inside the conversation, and they are outputs in Claude rather than saved files on your systems. To keep the checklist, copy the content out into wherever it needs to live, or keep the conversation somewhere you can find it again. Do not treat the pane as permanent storage.
Verify before you circulate

Because Claude generates the content, treat the checklist as a strong draft, not a finished source of truth. This is the same reason to check any AI output that you met in the general track: fluent and confident is not the same as correct. Before it goes to a new starter, confirm the access requests, the named owners, and any dates are actually right for how your team works. That final read is the part only you can give, whether or not you manage anyone.

title: Artifacts and structured output

content_blocks.text: What actually happens to what you type

Every time you paste something into Claude, you are handing it to a system that runs outside your own machine. It helps to have a clear picture of what that means. Claude is a chat assistant: it reads what you give it, responds, and does not go looking through your files or your inbox on its own. The risk here is lighter than with tools that plug directly into your live company data. But lighter is not none, and the one decision that matters is the same every time: what you choose to put in the box.

The general track already covered why you verify AI output and never treat fluent text as fact. This lesson is narrower. It is about the input side: what you share with Claude before it ever responds.
The one judgement call: is this yours to share

Most of what you would naturally bring to Claude is fine. A public product description, a blog draft, a meeting agenda, a chunk of text you wrote and would happily forward to a colleague: paste it and get on with the work. The question only gets sharp when the content is not yet public and not yet yours to move around freely.

Take a concrete pair. You want Claude to tighten the wording of two documents. One is next quarter's results memo, still under embargo, full of numbers the market has not seen. The other is the public description of the same product on your website. The second one is safe to paste without a second thought. The first is exactly the kind of thing to hold back, or strip down, until you know your organisation is comfortable with it going to an external tool.

Treat an external AI tool the way you treat any system outside your company walls. If a document would need approval before you emailed it to someone outside the organisation, it needs the same approval before you paste it into Claude.
A quick test before you paste

You do not need a policy memorised to make this call. Ask yourself one thing: if this text ended up somewhere I did not intend, would that be a problem. If the honest answer is yes, do not paste it as-is. Usually you have a cleaner option anyway: give Claude the shape of the problem without the sensitive specifics.

For the results memo, that might mean pasting the structure and the wording you want help with while replacing the actual figures with placeholders. Claude can improve the phrasing of a sentence without knowing whether the number is nine or ninety. You keep the confidential part on your side and still get the help.

cards.body: Public or already-shared material: product descriptions, published docs, your own drafts, anything you could forward externally without approval.

cards.body: Unreleased financials, customer records, personal data, credentials, anything under embargo or NDA. Remove or mask the sensitive specifics, then ask for help on what remains.
cards.title: Pause and strip first

cards.body: Secrets that would cause real harm if exposed: passwords, API keys, security details. There is no version of these that belongs in a chat box.

content_blocks.text: Where the individual contributor stands

This is not only a management concern. You do not need a team or a title to be the person holding a sensitive document at the moment it matters. The colleague drafting the embargoed memo, the analyst with the raw customer list, the developer with a config file full of keys: each of them makes this call alone, at their own keyboard. Knowing where the line sits is part of doing the work well, not a rule handed down from above.

Your organisation may run Claude under a business or enterprise agreement with its own data-handling terms, which can differ from the consumer version. Confirm which one you are using and what its terms say before deciding what is acceptable to share.
What you can now do

You can tell at a glance which documents are safe to hand Claude and which need masking or approval first. You can get real help on sensitive material by sharing its shape without its secrets. And you know to check your own organisation's terms rather than assume. Next you will meet Claude Cowork, where Claude connects to your actual tools and data, and this input-side judgement matters more, not less.

content_blocks.text: You have a grant application due Friday, and the pieces already exist. A previous submission to work from, a budget spreadsheet, the programme write-up, a page of impact figures, and the funder's guidelines. Assembling them into one coherent bid is the actual job. In plain browser chat, that job starts with a chore: open each file, copy it, paste it into the conversation, then do the same for the next one before Claude can even see the full set. A spreadsheet often will not paste cleanly at all. Claude Cowork removes that opening chore. It reads the files where they already sit.
What Cowork actually is

Claude Cowork is Claude with reach beyond the conversation. It started as a desktop application and has since expanded to the browser and to mobile, so you are not tied to one device to use it. On desktop, you bring it up with a keyboard shortcut from wherever you happen to be working, and it can read the files and folders on your machine that you give it access to, and look at what is on your screen when you ask it to. The model underneath is the same Claude you have used in the browser. What changes is its reach. It can work with what is already in front of you, without you copying anything in.

That reach is the reason the previous lesson on what you share matters here. Because Cowork can read your screen and open local files, it can pick up far more than you meant to hand over in one go. Invoke it deliberately, and keep it pointed at only the files the task actually needs.
Where it beats plain chat

Go back to the grant application. In the browser, the friction is not the writing, it is the ferrying: every source document has to be copied in before Claude can use it. With Cowork, you gather the documents together, point it at them, and ask it to draft the bid from the whole set. It reads all of them in place. The minutes you would otherwise spend shuttling content between windows simply go away.

The same pattern holds for any task where the material is spread across several files or already open on your screen. Reconciling three versions of a report, pulling figures out of a spreadsheet into a summary, drafting a reply to the message you are looking at. Whenever the work is really about combining things you already have, rather than one clean question, Cowork is the version that fits.
How it sits alongside Claude.ai

Cowork does not replace Claude.ai. They share a model, and both keep your Projects and your history. Cowork now runs on desktop, in the browser, and on mobile (the browser and mobile versions are in beta), so the real difference is not which device you are on. It is what each one can reach.

content_blocks.text: When to stay in the browser

Not every job wants screen access. A long, focused session, structuring a proposal from a blank page or thinking through a decision over many turns, is still served well by the browser and its full conversation history. Cowork earns its place on the quick, in-between jobs that touch what is already open: summarise this, draft that, tell me what I am looking at.

If you lead a team, the tasks worth pointing people at Cowork first are the repetitive assembly jobs that quietly eat afternoons: the monthly report stitched together from five exports, the bid built from last cycle's documents. If you have no reports, the same test works on your own week. The next time you catch yourself copying a third file into a chat, that is the moment Cowork was built for.

title: What Claude Cowork is and when to use it

content_blocks.text:
Most of the value in Cowork shows up in the back-and-forth, not in the first reply. You rarely get the final version of anything on the first attempt, and you are not meant to. This lesson is about running a working session well: keeping one thread going as you refine, giving Claude the context once so it carries across, and moving the finished work into whatever application it needs to live in.

The running example throughout is a half-day workshop agenda you are shaping and reshaping until it holds together.
Keep one thread going

The most useful habit in a working session is to stay in the same conversation while you refine, rather than starting fresh for each change.

Say you ask Claude for a first draft of the agenda. You read it back and react: the morning is too dense, the group is senior so the introductions can go, and there should be a working break before lunch. Because you are still in the same thread, you do not re-paste the agenda to make those changes. Claude already has the current version in view and edits from there. Each round builds on the last, so by the fourth or fifth pass you are adjusting timings and wording, not re-explaining the whole thing.

How to phrase that feedback well is prompting craft, and the general track already covers it. What matters here is the mechanic: one continuous thread is what lets your earlier decisions accumulate instead of evaporating.

A long thread can also turn against you. If you switch to a genuinely different task, the old context becomes noise and can pull answers off course. The general track lesson on starting fresh versus keeping going is the guide here. A good rule: one thread per thing you are shaping.
Give Claude the context once

For work you return to across several sessions, load the shared context once instead of rebuilding it every time you open a chat. Two features do most of this work.

A Project holds the material Claude should always have in view for a body of work. For the workshop, you might create a Project and add the objectives, the list of who is attending and their roles, and last quarter's agenda for reference. From then on, every conversation you start inside that Project already has that background, so a new thread does not mean a cold start.

Global instructions are the standing preferences that apply everywhere: your role, the kind of output you want, the language to default to. You write them once and Claude carries them into every session. Keep them to what you actually need. They are persistent context, not a biography.

If you notice yourself giving Claude the same shaping instructions on task after task, that repeated instruction is worth saving as a Skill, the named instruction set you met earlier in the track. Skills work in Cowork too, so keep noticing the candidates as they come up and save the ones that recur.
Iterating together across surfaces
Cowork is not only the desktop window. Claude can work inside the tools where the work already lives, so you can refine in place rather than copying text back and forth.

The Chrome extension reads the content of whatever page is open, and the Microsoft 365 integration works with what is in front of you. Before you invoke either on sensitive material, check that it is covered by your organisation's AI data policy. The safe-use lesson in this module goes into this properly.
Where Claude sits next to Copilot in M365

If your organisation also runs Microsoft Copilot, the two are not interchangeable, and the Copilot track covers when to reach for which in depth. In short, Copilot has deep access to your Microsoft 365 data and is stronger when the task needs it to search across your inbox, calendar, or files. Claude is stronger when you want a specific output format or the skills and instructions you have already set up. For shaping the agenda, where the value is in the iteration and the format, Claude is the natural fit.
What you can now do

You can run a proper working session in Cowork: hold one thread while you iterate, set up a Project and global instructions so context persists instead of being retyped, and carry the same work across the desktop app, Chrome, and Microsoft 365. That is the difference between using Claude for one-off answers and using it as something you actually work alongside.

content_blocks.text: MCP is the standard you met in the general track: the open protocol that lets an assistant reach your other tools and data directly, instead of waiting for you to paste things in. Cowork is where you put it to work. On its own, Cowork works with the files you point it at and can look at what is on your screen when you ask. Connect it to a tool such as your calendar or a shared folder, and it can go and fetch what it needs by itself. This lesson shows how to make those connections, what one connection unlocks, and where to be careful.
What a connection adds

Take a job you probably repeat every week: pulling together a stand-up brief for your team. Normally you open the calendar to see who is in and what is scheduled, glance at the shared project folder for the latest status notes, and stitch the two into a short summary. Connect Cowork to that calendar and that folder once, and you can ask for the brief directly. It reads the coming week from the calendar, pulls the recent files from the folder, and drafts the summary. You check it and send it.

If you do not run the stand-up yourself, the same two connections still earn their place. Point them at your own week and the group you sit in, and Cowork assembles your personal brief the same way.
The saving is not the drafting, which Cowork could already do from pasted text. It is removing the gather step: the tabs you open and the copying you do before you can even ask.
Making a connection

Open the connections settings in Cowork and choose the tool you want to add. Sign in to that tool when prompted, and confirm the access it requests. Once authorised, the connection stays available across your sessions, so this is a one-time setup rather than something you repeat each morning.

Connections vary in what they grant. Some are read-only: Cowork can see the calendar or the folder but change nothing. Others can also act, such as sending a message or editing a file. Note which kind you are enabling, because the second kind is doing things on your behalf.
Check before you connect
A connection is a standing grant of access, so it is worth a moment of thought before you confirm it. Three questions cover most of the risk.

cards.body: A connector scoped to one shared folder has far less reach than one that can see your whole drive or mailbox. Prefer the narrower scope when the task allows it.
cards.title: What can it read?

cards.body: Read-only connectors are lower risk than ones that can send, edit, or delete. Know which you are granting before you confirm.
cards.title: What can it do?

cards.body: Connectors from Anthropic or a vendor already in your approved stack are safer than an unknown or community one. If the source is unclear, do not connect it to work data.
cards.title: Who built it?

content_blocks.text: The same care applies to what you feed a connection over time. Keep a connected project scoped to one piece of work, and when that work ends, remove connections and files that no longer belong there so context does not carry over into the next thing.

A connector can pull in client data, personal data, or commercially sensitive material without you copying it in by hand. That convenience is exactly why you check your organisation's AI data policy covers the source before you connect it, not after.
Verify what it assembles

Because a connection lets Cowork gather inputs on its own, you are no longer watching every piece go in. That is the point of it, but it also means the output deserves a read before it leaves you. Skim the stand-up brief against the calendar and the folder: did it catch the meeting that moved, and use the latest status note rather than last week's?

This is the same reason you met in the general track for checking any AI output. Fluent text is not evidence that it is right or complete, and a connection that fetches its own data does not change that. It just makes the quick check the last step rather than an optional one.
What you can now do

You can connect Cowork to a tool, judge whether that connection is safe to grant, and use it to remove the gathering work from a recurring task. The stand-up brief is one example; any job where you assemble the same few sources into the same short output is a candidate for the same setup.

content_blocks.text: You have 200 survey files sitting in one folder, exported one at a time, each named something like "export_final_v2 (3).csv". They need renaming to a consistent scheme and sorting into subfolders by region and quarter. By hand, that is a lost afternoon and at least three quiet mistakes. This is the shape of work Claude Code is built for: not a single answer to a single question, but a multi-step job carried out over real files on your machine.
Where Claude Code fits

In the general track you met the idea of an agent: an AI that plans and takes several steps towards a goal with some autonomy, rather than answering once and stopping. Claude Code is that idea made concrete and pointed at operational work. It runs on your computer, reads the files in front of it, and carries out a task step by step until the job is done.

That is what separates it from the Claude you have used in a browser. Claude chat is where you think, draft, and analyse: you bring the text, it gives text back, and nothing on your machine changes. Claude Code acts. On the survey folder, it renames the files, moves them into the right subfolders, and shows you exactly what it changed.

Claude Code opens in whatever folder you point it at, and that folder becomes its workspace. You do not need to be a command-line expert to use it. You need to know which folder holds the files you want worked on.
The agent loop

Hand Claude Code the survey folder and it does not fire off one command and hope. It works a loop: it reads what is actually there, proposes a plan, carries out the steps, checks the results, and then either finishes or comes back to you with a question. On these files that means it spots the three different naming patterns you did not know were mixed in, tells you before it touches anything, and asks how you want the odd ones handled.

You are the director here. You decide what the task is, you approve the plan, and you judge whether the result is right. Claude Code does the work; the judgement stays with you.

Before it runs anything that changes your files, Claude Code shows you what it intends to do and waits for your approval. That checkpoint is where you catch a confident but wrong plan, for the same reason the general track drilled in: a fluent plan is not a correct one.
What this is and is not

Claude Code can also write and run software, and if shipping an application is your goal, the developer track is where that lives. The frame worth holding here is narrower and fits far more people: an automation and operations assistant. The jobs it earns its place on are the repetitive, multi-file, multi-step ones you currently grind through by hand.

content_blocks.text: If you manage a team, the payoff is obvious: the afternoon this task would have cost someone is handed back. If you are the one who currently does it, that afternoon is handed back to you. Either way, the skill is spotting which tasks are worth handing over, so your attention goes to the work only you can do.
What it cannot do

It makes mistakes. It will occasionally misread a pattern or misunderstand what you asked, which is why you verify the output rather than trust it. By default it works only on what is in the folder you opened; reaching out to a database, Airtable, or a SharePoint site needs a connector, which is the MCP work covered earlier in this track. And it does not remember between sessions unless you give it standing context, covered later in this module.

Do not point Claude Code at the only copy of files you cannot afford to lose. Work on a copy, or ask it to write results into a new folder and leave the originals untouched, until you trust how a particular task behaves.
What comes next

You now have the frame: Claude Code is the general-track agent applied to files, data, and knowledge work, with you directing and verifying at each step. The next lesson gets hands-on with that survey folder and the everyday file and data tasks like it, so the loop stops being a description and becomes something you have run yourself.
