title: Governed, safe use, DLP and connectors

content_blocks.text: You have a real job in mind now, so build it. The task for this lesson is a small app that lets someone on a site log a safety observation from their phone, note what they saw, attach a photo, and have it land in a shared list the safety team already watches. It is a good first canvas app: one clear user, one data source, a handful of screens. This walks you through it end to end, and it flags the one thing that most often breaks first-time apps.
Pick and scope before you open the tool

A well-scoped canvas app has three to seven screens, one or two data sources, and simple create-and-read logic. Our observation app fits that comfortably: a list of recent observations, a form to add a new one, and a confirmation. One role, one list.

Write down the fields before you build anything. For a safety observation that is roughly: what was seen, where, how serious, who logged it, when, and a photo. Those become the columns in your list, and everything downstream depends on getting them right first.

Resist the urge to add "just one more thing" at this stage. An app that logs observations is useful on Monday. An app that also assigns actions, tracks closure, and emails managers is a different, much larger project. Ship the small one first.
Build the list first, then the app

The data comes before the interface. Create a list in SharePoint (or Microsoft Lists, which is the same list) with the columns you wrote down. Use the column types SharePoint gives you: single line of text for the description, a choice column for severity, a date column, a person column for who logged it.

With the list in place, the fastest no-code route is to let Power Apps generate the app from it. Sign in to make.powerapps.com, select **Start with data**, choose **SharePoint**, enter your site URL, connect, then pick your observations list and select **Create app**.

Power Apps Studio opens with a working three-screen app already built against your list.

cards.body: A scrollable gallery of every observation in the list. This is what the safety team lands on.
cards.title: Browse screen

cards.body: One observation shown in full, opened by tapping an item in the gallery.
cards.title: Details screen

cards.body: The form for logging a new observation or correcting an existing one. This is the screen a site worker uses most.
cards.title: Edit screen

content_blocks.text: That generated app is a working, connected starting point rather than a blank canvas. You shape it from here instead of building from nothing, which saves you most of the setup.
Shape the screens for a phone

Two changes make this genuinely usable on site. First, add photo capture to the edit screen. Power Apps has an Add picture control that lets someone take a photo with the phone camera or choose an existing one; drop it onto the edit form and bind it to your list so the image saves with the record.

Second, trim the edit form to only the fields a worker fills in. Remove anything auto-set (the logger and the timestamp can be filled by a formula rather than typed) so the person on site sees the shortest form that does the job.

Confirm the exact camera or image control and how it writes back to your list against current Power Apps documentation before you rely on it. Saving photos to SharePoint has specific handling, and the control names and behaviour shift between releases. Do not assume a click-path you have not seen on screen.

The generated form already saves records for you when someone submits it, so you do not need to write formula logic for a basic version. If you later want a field set automatically, that is where Power Fx (Excel-style formulas placed directly on a control) comes in, but a working first app does not require it.
Verify it, and watch for the trap

Preview the app inside the studio, log a test observation, and check the record actually appears in your SharePoint list. Then open it on a phone through the Power Apps mobile app and log one for real, photo and all. Testing on the device it will be used on is not optional for a mobile app.

Here is the tool-specific trap, and you met its name in your first build: delegation. Your app will look perfect in testing with a dozen records and then quietly return incomplete results once the list grows to thousands. For large lists, Power Apps only processes records up to a set limit unless your filter and sort functions are ones the data source can handle itself, and when a formula is not delegable it shows a yellow warning icon on it.

Treat that yellow delegation warning as a real signal, not a cosmetic one. On a list that stays small it rarely bites. On one that grows, it means records past the limit are silently dropped from what your app shows, and nobody notices until a real observation goes missing.
For a safety log that could accumulate for years, keep your gallery filters simple and delegable, or plan to move to a data source with broader delegation support if the volume climbs.
Publish, share, reflect

When it works, save and publish from the studio, then share it with the site team or a security group. Embedding the app as a tab in the Microsoft Teams channel the team already uses is the most practical option for internal tools, because sign-in is handled and nobody has a new URL to remember.

Then reflect on the loop you just ran: you picked a real task, scoped it to one list and a few screens, generated and shaped the app, and verified it on the actual device. That loop is the same whatever the app does. The judgment that matters is not clicking through the studio; it is scoping tightly enough that the app stays maintainable and spotting the delegation limit before it costs you a record.

content_blocks.text: This app is deliberately half a solution. Logging observations is the front end; what happens to a serious one after it is logged is automation. The next lesson combines this app with a Power Automate flow so a high-severity observation routes to the right person without anyone chasing it.

title: Building a no-code app with Power Apps

content_blocks.text:
Until now you have built the two halves apart. In Band 2 you made a flow that ran on its own, and in the last lesson you built an app that stood on its own. This capstone joins them. You are going to build a small system where an app captures something and an automation acts on it. The interesting work is the seam between them.

The task is a training request. Someone fills in a short app: what course, why, roughly what it costs. The moment they submit, a flow picks it up, sends it to their manager for approval, and emails the requester the outcome. No one copies anything from one place to another. This is what separates owning two tools from running a platform.
Pick a task where the handoff is the point

Choose something in your own work that has a capture step and a routing step. A training request works because it has both: a person supplies information, then that information needs to travel to someone else and come back with a decision. Expense pre-approval, equipment requests, and access requests all share the shape.

Avoid anything where the decision has real legal or financial weight for a first build. You want a process where a wrong route or a missed notification is an annoyance, not an incident. Training requests sit comfortably there.
Scope it: design the shared table first

Here is the part that separates a platform from two disconnected toys. The app and the flow do not talk to each other directly. They meet in a data source, and that data source is the contract between them. Get it right before you build either half.

Sketch the fields the whole system needs, not just the ones the form shows. For the training request you need what the requester types (course name, reason, estimated cost, their manager) and what the flow writes back (a status, and maybe a decision note). The status field is the channel: the app sets it to Pending on submit, the flow changes it to Approved or Rejected, and the app reads it back so the requester can see where things stand.

Design the status field as a fixed choice set (Pending, Approved, Rejected), not free text. Both halves read and write it, and a typo like "Aproved" that the flow never matches is the kind of bug that only shows up in front of a real requester.

Create this table once, in a data source both tools can reach. In Power Platform that is typically a Dataverse table or a SharePoint list. Whichever you pick, create it before you open Power Apps or Power Automate, because both will point at it.
Build the app half

Build the capture app against that table, the same way you did in the previous lesson. Bind the form to the shared table. Show the fields the requester fills in, and set the status field to Pending automatically on submit rather than asking the person to choose it. They should never see or set their own approval status.

Keep the app honest about what it does not control. The requester submits and then waits; the app cannot show an outcome that has not happened yet. A simple read-only view of their past requests with the current status is enough, and it is the payoff for wiring the status field through both halves.
Build the automation half

Now the flow. Its trigger is the seam: it should fire when a new row lands in the shared table, so submitting the app is what starts the automation. In Power Automate this is a "when a new item is created" style trigger pointed at the same table the app writes to.

The middle of the flow is an approval. Power Automate has a built-in approval action that sends a request to a named person and waits for their response before continuing. Feed it the manager captured on the request. When the response comes back, the flow writes the outcome to the status field and sends the requester an email with the result.

If your flow triggers on any change to a row and also writes back to that same row, it can trigger itself in a loop. Trigger on creation only, or add a condition so the flow ignores rows that already have a decision. Test this before you leave it running; a loop can fire a lot of approvals fast.
Verify the two halves as one system

Do not test the app and the flow separately and call it done. The whole reason you built this is the handoff, so verify the handoff. Submit a real request through the app using a test account, then watch the flow run history to confirm it triggered, check the approval actually reached the manager, respond to it, and confirm both the email arrived and the status updated back in the app.

Run the rejection path too, not just the happy one. A system that only works when everyone says yes is half-tested. Reject a request and confirm the requester is told clearly, and that the app reflects Rejected rather than sitting on Pending.

Approvals route to real inboxes and Teams. During testing, point the manager field at yourself or a test account so you are not sending live approval requests to a colleague who has no idea what your capstone is.

content_blocks.text: Package it as one thing

The lesson title calls this a combined solution for a reason. In Power Platform a solution is a container that holds the app and the flow together, along with the table if you built it in Dataverse, so they move and deploy as a unit rather than loose pieces someone has to reassemble. Building your capstone inside one solution from the start means you can hand the whole system to someone else, or promote it from a test environment to a live one, without leaving a half behind.
Reflect

Step back and notice what the integration actually required. The hard part was not building an app or building a flow; you could already do both. It was agreeing the shared table up front so the two halves spoke the same language, and being disciplined about which half owns which field. The app owns what the requester says. The flow owns the decision. The status field is where they meet.

That pattern travels. Any time a capture step needs to trigger a routed decision and report back, it is the same three moves: a shared table, a trigger on the write, and a status the automation owns and the app reads. Even with no one reporting to you, you have just built something that used to need a person forwarding emails, and you can point it at the next manual handoff on your own list.

content_blocks.text: What Obsidian is and when it helps

Say you have been tracking a competitor for months. Every earnings call, every quiet pricing change, every product launch you noticed went into a note. Six months in, that running scan is worth more than any single entry in it. The real question is whether anything can read the whole pile back to you when a planning meeting lands on your calendar. That gap is what Obsidian is built for.
A different kind of note tool

Obsidian stores each note as a plain text file on your own computer, written in a lightweight format called markdown. There is no proprietary database behind it and no cloud account you have to depend on. A note is just a `.md` file you can open, move, back up, or hand to another tool. Most note apps you have used do not work this way. OneNote keeps its notes in a format only Microsoft can read, and Notion keeps everything on its own servers.

That sounds like a small technical detail. It is the reason the rest of this matters.
Why plain files matter now

Because your notes are ordinary files, anything that can read files can read them, including the AI assistants you met earlier in this path. Point one at your competitive scan and it can search every note at once, pull together what you know about a rival before a strategy session, or surface the pricing moves you logged back in January and had half forgotten. No export step, no copy-paste, no reformatting. The prediction engine works on text, and your vault is text.

Connecting an assistant to your vault uses the same connection standard you met in the general track, and a later lesson in this track shows the mechanics. For now, the point is simpler: the format your notes are in decides whether an AI tool can help you with them at all.

Connecting an assistant to a folder does not quietly upload it. You choose which folder to open for a given task, and nothing leaves your machine until you do. Apply the same judgement you would give any sensitive document before you point a tool at your notes.
The part that compounds

One good note is a reminder to yourself. A vault you have added to for months is context. The scan you started in spring can answer a question in autumn that you did not think to ask when you wrote it. Every note you add raises the quality of the next question you put to an assistant.
When Obsidian is not the answer

Obsidian is a personal thinking space, not a collaboration tool. Anything a team needs to edit together belongs in SharePoint or Teams, and Obsidian does not replace them. It is not a project manager and not your company knowledge base. What it takes over is the notebook nobody else ever opened, the notes you were keeping only for yourself. If your competitive scan is really a shared team document, keep it where the team can reach it. If it is your own read on the market, that is the work Obsidian is for.

content_blocks.text: You just came out of a project meeting with a page of scribbled decisions and a short list of things someone now has to do. This lesson takes you from nothing installed to that meeting captured as a clean note in Obsidian, with headings for each section and a tickable checklist for the actions. By the end you will have a working vault and know the handful of markdown that fills it.
Install and open your first vault

Obsidian is free to download from obsidian.md and installs like any other application on Windows or Mac. You do not need to create an account to start.

The first time you open it, Obsidian asks you to create or open a vault. A vault is just a folder on your computer that Obsidian treats as your knowledge base, so this step is really about choosing where your notes will live. Pick a location that is easy to find and gets backed up. Your Documents folder synced through OneDrive works well. Avoid burying the vault in a deeply nested, IT-managed path. The folder name is only a name, and you can rename it later.

Obsidian does not back up your vault for you on the free version. Because the vault is just a folder of files, put it somewhere your normal backup already covers, like OneDrive. The built-in Obsidian Sync is a paid add-on you do not need for this.
Find your way around

With a vault open, you are looking at three areas: a file list on the left, the editor in the middle where you write, and a side panel on the right you can ignore for now. That is the whole interface you need today.
Capture the meeting as a note

Create a new note (Ctrl+N on Windows, Cmd+N on Mac). The title you type becomes the filename, so name it something you will recognise later, such as `Project kickoff 2026-07-02`. Consistent, dated titles make notes easy to sort now and easy for an AI assistant to filter when you point one at your vault in a later lesson.

Then type the meeting straight into the editor. A note is a plain markdown file, which means you format it with a few text symbols instead of a toolbar.
The markdown you actually need

You met markdown in the general track, so here is only how it behaves inside Obsidian, using the meeting note as the example.

A single `#` at the start of a line gives you the note title. Two, `##`, marks each section, so you might have `## Decisions` and `## Action items`. A hyphen at the start of a line, `- like this`, makes a bullet. Wrapping text in double asterisks, `**like this**`, makes it bold.

For the action items, write each one as a task rather than a plain bullet: `- [ ] confirm the vendor pricing with Sara`. Obsidian turns `- [ ]` into a checkbox you can click to tick off, and it shows as `- [x]` once done. That is the piece worth remembering here, because it turns a list of things to do into something you can actually work through after the meeting.

You will also see links written as `[[Note name]]`. Those are how notes connect to each other, and the next lesson on linking and structure is where that belongs, so leave it aside for now.
What to skip for now

Obsidian has a large plugin ecosystem, a graph view, and deep customisation. Almost none of it matters in your first week. The graph view, community plugins, templates, and the paid Sync feature can all wait. The tool rewards writing notes, not configuring them, and the real trap is spending more time tuning the setup than using it.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can install Obsidian, create a vault in a sensible location, and capture a real meeting as a structured note with headings and a working checklist. That is a complete note-taking loop. The next lesson shows how to connect notes to each other so your vault becomes more than a folder of separate files.

title: Getting started, notes and markdown

content_blocks.text: You have a folder of notes now. This lesson turns that folder into something you can actually move through: notes that point to each other, and just enough structure that the right context is one click away when you come back to it weeks later.
Linking one note to another

The core move in Obsidian is the link. Inside any note, type two square brackets and start typing a note title: `[[`. Obsidian shows a list of your existing notes as you type. Pick one, close the brackets, and you have a clickable link between the two notes.

Take a live example. You keep a note for a project you are running. During the project you make a call about which vendor to use, and you write that up in its own note. You also have a note for each person involved. From the project note, link out to all of them:

`See [[March vendor decision]] and the owners [[Priya Shah]] and [[Tom Green]].`

Now the project note is a hub. When you open it in three months to brief someone or write a summary, you do not have to remember where the decision lives or who signed off. You follow the links.

If you link to a note that does not exist yet, Obsidian keeps the link as a placeholder and creates the note the moment you click it. So you can link to `[[March vendor decision]]` before you have written it, then fill it in later. The connection is already in place.
Links go one way as you type them, but Obsidian tracks them both ways. On the decision note you can see everything that points to it, so you do not have to add the link twice.
Tags for the things that cut across notes

A link connects two specific notes. A tag labels a note as belonging to a group, wherever that note happens to sit. You add one by writing a hash and a word anywhere in the note: `#decision`, `#meeting`, `#project/atlas`.

The point of tags is that one note can carry several, and a tag never moves the file. Your vendor decision note can be tagged `#decision` and `#project/atlas` at the same time. Later, when you want every decision you have made across all projects, you filter on `#decision` and they all surface, no matter which folder they live in.

Keep the set small at first. A handful of tags you actually reuse beats twenty you invent once and forget. Add a new one only when you notice yourself wanting it.

Links and tags work inside a single vault. A `[[link]]` resolves to a note in the same vault and will not reach a note in a different one. If you keep separate vaults for separate parts of your life, treat each as its own self-contained set.
Just enough structure

You do not need an elaborate folder tree, and building one before you have many notes usually means rebuilding it later. A light structure is enough: a folder or two for the areas you work in, and one note you treat as your way in.

That entry note, often called `Home` or `Index`, is the one note you open first. It links out to the things that matter: your active projects, your key reference notes. Without it, a growing vault becomes a flat pile you search through every time. With it, you have one starting point that you, or an AI assistant reading your vault later, can follow to reach everything else.

The order to remember is simple. The vault holds folders, folders hold notes, and links and tags run across all of them regardless of which folder a note sits in. Structure groups your notes; links and tags connect them.

None of this is busywork for its own sake. The next lesson connects an AI assistant to your vault, and a linked, lightly tagged vault is exactly what makes that useful. When notes point to each other and share consistent tags, an assistant reading the vault can follow the same trails you would: from a project to its decisions to the people involved. A pile of disconnected files gives it far less to work with.

content_blocks.text: Picture asking a plain question out loud: what did we actually decide about the supplier change back in spring? If your notes are scattered across chat threads and half-finished pages, you answer that by scrolling and guessing. If those same notes sit in a vault an AI assistant can read, you ask the assistant and it reads the relevant notes back to you. This lesson is about that shift, from searching your own memory to querying your own writing, and what it asks of the way you take notes.
How an assistant reads your vault

Your vault is a folder of plain text files. That is the whole mechanism. Any AI assistant that can reach your file system can open those files, search them, and reason over them, without you pasting anything into a chat. There is no special Obsidian integration to buy, no plugin to install, no API key to wire up.

You already met the connection models in the general track and in the other tool tracks, so we will not re-explain how an assistant gets access here. The point specific to Obsidian is smaller and more useful: because a vault is just files, making it readable to AI takes no extra work. If your notes exist as text, they are already in the format an assistant wants.

This is the quiet advantage of plain text. Notes locked in a proprietary format have to be exported or shared one page at a time before an assistant can use them. A vault skips that step entirely, which is why the readability question moves from "can it read this at all" to "is what I wrote clear enough to be worth reading".
What this changes about note-taking

The value of a note stops being only in writing it down. It becomes the ability to use it later, at speed, with help. A single note read back to you is a small convenience. Six months of notes an assistant can search across is a different kind of asset: a store of your decisions, your open questions, and your reasoning that any future question can draw on.

That effect compounds. The question you ask today benefits from the note you wrote in January, as long as January's note still makes sense out of context. This is where note-taking habits start to matter in a way they never did when you were the only reader who could fill in the gaps.
Writing notes an assistant can actually use

Here is the catch that the supplier-change question exposes. If the only trace of that decision is a note that reads "supplier change, maybe Q3?", an assistant reading your vault is as stuck as a colleague would be. It cannot tell whether that was decided, proposed, or dismissed. A chaotic scribble with abbreviations only you understand confuses an assistant for the same reason it confuses everyone else.

A few habits make your notes hold their meaning when they are read cold, months later, by something that was not in the room.

content_blocks.text: None of this means writing polished prose. The barrier to capturing a note should stay near zero, or you will stop capturing. It means spending the extra few words on the points you will want to retrieve, so the version of you asking the question later, and the assistant helping you, both get a clean answer.
A note on judgement

Your vault lives on your machine, and local files are not sent anywhere on their own. When you point an assistant at your vault, you are choosing to share specific notes for a specific task, and you decide what is in scope.

Apply the same judgement you would to any sensitive document. If a note holds confidential or personal information, think before you hand the folder that contains it to an external assistant. Readable does not mean everything should be read by everything. You control what you share and when, so use that control on purpose.
Where this leaves you

You do not have to manage a team to feel this. If you take notes only for yourself, the payoff is direct: the effort of writing one clear sentence today is repaid every time an assistant answers a question from it later without you digging. If you do lead a team, the same habits make your own record something you can query in seconds before a decision, rather than a place you avoid because you cannot find anything in it.

title: Using Obsidian with an AI assistant

content_blocks.text: Your vault is a folder of plain markdown files on your own machine. That is what makes Obsidian private by default, and it is also what you hand over to any sync service or plugin you switch on.

Two ordinary choices quietly move your notes beyond your own device: how you sync a vault across machines, and which community plugins you let read it. Neither is risky by nature. Both are worth a moment of thought once the vault holds sensitive material such as client notes, HR records, or unreleased plans.
Where your notes go when you sync

Obsidian keeps everything local until you decide otherwise. To read the same vault on your laptop and your phone, you either use Obsidian's own Sync service or point a general cloud tool such as iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive, or Google Drive at the vault folder.

The difference that matters for sensitive work is who can read the files once they leave your device. Obsidian Sync is designed so that only you hold the key and the provider stores encrypted data it cannot open. A general cloud folder is different: the files sit there in a form readable by whoever administers that account, including your IT team and the provider, under that service's own terms.

Before you put sensitive notes in any synced vault, check where that provider actually stores the data and whether that storage is allowed under your confidentiality agreements and your data policy. A vault syncing to a personal cloud account is often the exact thing those agreements forbid.
Community plugins can read the whole vault

Obsidian ships with community plugins switched off behind Restricted Mode. When you turn that off to install one, you are running third-party code inside your vault.

A plugin runs with the same reach you have. It can read every note in the vault, and many legitimately need to. It can also make network requests, which means a plugin is technically able to send vault content elsewhere. Most community plugins are open source and well behaved, but "most" is the operative word.

So treat installing a plugin as a small trust decision rather than a convenience click. A few checks before you enable one:

content_blocks.text:
You have set Obsidian up and learned to run it safely. Now you build something real with it, end to end. The task for this guided build is a vault for a professional certification you are studying for: the months-long kind of effort where notes pile up from courses, practice exams, and your own working-out, and where the whole pile is worthless if you cannot find the one thing you need the night before the test.

The shape is the same one every build in this path follows. You pick a real task, scope it, build it, verify it, and reflect. What makes this build its own thing is the last quality you will design for: a vault that an AI assistant can actually read and reason over. Getting there is less about clever plugins than about how you write.

If you manage a team studying for the same certification, the vault you build here is also a template you can hand them. The habits scale from one person revising alone to a group building shared knowledge.
Scope it before you touch a folder

Before you make a single folder, decide what you want to be able to do at the end. Not "organise my notes", which is a chore with no finish line, but something you can test. For a certification effort it might be: revise a weak exam domain in twenty minutes, or ask an AI assistant to quiz you on the areas you keep getting wrong.

Scope is what keeps you from building an elaborate system you abandon in a fortnight. Write the one or two outcomes down. Everything you build should serve them, and anything that does not is decoration.
Build the folder skeleton

Start with a flat top level and a clear logic behind each folder. A hybrid model works well here: one place for raw capture, one for the live material organised by exam domain, one for the concepts that outlast any single study session, and one for reusable resources. A simple log for daily study notes rounds it off.

cards.body: Where everything lands first when you are moving fast. You process it later, so you never have to make a filing decision mid-lecture. The most important folder in the vault.
cards.title: Inbox

cards.body: The exam areas, one folder each. Practice-test reviews, worked problems, and notes tied to a specific part of the syllabus live here while you are actively revising.
cards.title: Domains

cards.body: Evergreen explanations in your own words. This is the knowledge that stays useful after the exam and the folder worth investing your best writing in.
cards.title: Concepts

cards.body: Things you reference but do not rewrite: templates, a formula sheet, links to source material. Keep it separate from the notes you actively edit.
cards.title: Resources

content_blocks.text: Prefix folders with two-digit numbers and gaps, such as 00 Inbox, 10 Domains, 20 Concepts, 30 Resources, so Obsidian sorts them in the order you work rather than alphabetically, and you can slot new folders in later without renaming everything. And do not create a folder until you have at least three notes that belong in it. If you hesitate for more than a few seconds about where a note goes, the structure has a gap or an overlap. Fix that before it compounds.
Capture notes that survive to exam night

The easiest thing to do is paste: copy the lecture transcript, drop in the slide export, screenshot the practice question. It feels productive and it saves you nothing. You still have to read the whole transcript later to find the one idea that mattered.

Ask a sharper question before writing a note: what would I want to find here the week before the exam? If the honest answer is the three concepts you got wrong on the mock test and why, write a note on those three. Three habits make the capture worth keeping.

Write in complete sentences for anything that matters. "Subnet mask thing, revisit" is meaningless in a month. "I keep confusing the broadcast address with the network address; the network address is the first in the range, the broadcast is the last" is still useful when you have forgotten you ever struggled with it. Date the note, so you can tell early confusion from a genuine gap that persisted. And state the so-what in one line: what this means for how you will answer that kind of question.

Capture is easy; processing is the actual work. Set aside a short window, ten minutes at the end of a study session, to turn raw captures into one or two clean notes. One good note pulled from a week of scribbles beats a hundred you never revisit.
Link concepts so revision compounds

Folders tell you where a note lives. Links tell you how ideas connect, and for exam revision that connection is where the value sits. Obsidian uses double square brackets for internal links, so writing the name of another note inside `[[...]]` creates a live link to it.

The move that pays off: when a practice-exam review exposes a weakness, link it to the concept note behind it. Over a few weeks, the concept notes that collect the most incoming links are exactly your recurring blind spots. That pattern is invisible in a folder list and obvious once the links are there.

Link with intent. A link is a claim that two ideas are related, so make it when the connection saves you a future search or reveals a pattern, and skip it when two notes merely share a word. Tags are the better tool for broad grouping such as a status of revised or shaky; links are for the specific relationships between ideas.
Templates for the notes you write again and again

If you are typing the same headings for the third time, template them. For a certification vault, two templates earn their keep almost immediately: a practice-exam review and a concept note. Keep each one lean, just the sections you always want, because a template you skip fields in is one you will stop using.

A practice-exam review template might be nothing more than a date line and headings for Score, What I got wrong, Why, and What to revise. The headings act as a checklist that stops you writing a vague "did okay" and moving on.

Obsidian has a built-in Templates feature, and the community plugin Templater does more. Templater can run small snippets so a note fills its own date on creation, for example `<% tp.date.now("YYYY-MM-DD") %>`, and place your cursor where you want to start typing. You do not need to write any code to benefit; the date and cursor features alone cover most of the need.

Templater is a community plugin, so it runs third-party code. Install it from the community plugins area only after the safe-use checks you learned in the previous lesson, and point its template folder at your Resources folder. Verify the current plugin name and settings against Obsidian before you rely on a specific menu path.
Make it readable to an AI assistant

This is the part specific to Obsidian, and it puts to work what the earlier lesson on using Obsidian with an AI assistant showed you. It is the reason the writing habits above are not just tidiness. Because every note is a plain markdown file on your own machine, an AI assistant that can read your files (through the file access you met in the general track) can work directly with your vault. It can quiz you, summarise your weak domains, or draft a revision plan from your notes.

But readable is not the same as useful. An assistant reading your vault has no memory of anything outside the text you give it. It cannot guess what a cryptic abbreviation meant or which exam domain a loose note belongs to. It reads what is there, the way a stranger would. The way you write is what closes that gap.

Use clear headings, so the assistant can tell a decision from background. Name things with a brief clarifier the first time, so "CIDR (the notation for IP address ranges)" carries its own meaning. Make relationships explicit in words, not only links, because "this follows from the routing rules in my Networking concept note" travels with the text even when the assistant is reading one file. And add a date and a status line to the notes you lean on, so it can tell current understanding from something you have since superseded.

For the handful of notes you will query most, a small block of structured metadata at the very top helps. Between two lines of three dashes, add a few fields such as date, domain, and status. An assistant can read that block and answer a request like "summarise my shaky topics in the networking domain" with precision.

An AI assistant can only hold so much text in view at once, the context window from the general track. Do not point it at your whole vault and hope. Ask it to read one folder, such as your networking domain, and it will do far better. This is why curated concept notes beat a hundred raw transcripts: you are handing over knowledge, not a haystack.
Verify the build

You scoped this vault around one or two outcomes. Now test them against reality rather than assuming the build worked.

Take the coldest test first. Open one concept note and read it as if you had never seen it, with no memory of the study session behind it. If a reference is opaque or you cannot tell when you wrote it, that is the note failing the AI test too, because the assistant sees the same thing you just saw. Fix the missing context.

Then run the real thing. Ask your assistant a genuine question against one folder: "read my networking domain notes and quiz me on what I get wrong most." If the answer is sharp and specific, your notes are. If it is vague and generic, the notes are vague, and no prompt will rescue them. The quality of the output tracks the quality of what you wrote.
Reflect

You have built a vault that holds up under pressure and hands clean context to an AI. The deeper takeaway is that writing for your future self and writing for an assistant turned out to be the same discipline: dated notes, named things, explicit connections, curated rather than dumped.

Think about the last exam or deadline you prepared for. What did you wish you had written down at the start but did not? Picture the note that would have held it, and write your next one that way.

title: Build a structured vault, guided build

content_blocks.text:
Most of the tools you have met so far help you think, write, or find things faster. Lovable is a different kind of tool: you describe the app you want in plain language, and it builds working software you can open in a browser and share with other people.

That is the shift worth holding onto. You describe an outcome in plain words and get back something that actually runs, without writing code or filling in a template.
Where Lovable fits

You already know the difference between a job that needs a document and a job that needs a small tool other people will use. Lovable is for the second kind. When the thing you need is not a summary or a draft but a place where a few colleagues enter information and see it laid out, that is when Lovable earns its place.

Take the internal tool you keep meaning to build. Say the quarterly objectives your team sets each cycle live in a spreadsheet nobody enjoys opening, and half the entries have gone stale by week three. What you actually want is a simple page where each person adds their objectives and everyone can see them together. Historically that meant a developer, a backlog, and a wait. Lovable lets you describe that page and have a working version in front of you the same afternoon.

Lovable produces real software, which means it carries real consequences. Before you share an app that collects anything sensitive, or point colleagues at it as the source of truth, treat it the way you would any tool going live: check what it stores, who can see it, and whether it does what you claimed. A confident-looking app can still be wrong.
When to reach for it, and when not

cards.body: A small, well-scoped tool a handful of people will use: collecting inputs, showing them back, a light internal workflow. You can describe what it should do in a few plain sentences.
cards.title: A good fit

cards.body: A one-off answer, a document, or analysis you need once. If nobody has to use it as software afterwards, a chat assistant or a spreadsheet gets you there faster than building an app.
cards.title: Reach for something else

content_blocks.text: If you lead a team, the same instinct covers the small tools you would never get budget to commission. If you do not, it covers the ones you would otherwise build by hand in a spreadsheet and maintain forever. Either way the judgement is the same: has this job quietly turned into a tool other people will use?

The skill this module builds is not learning to drive every button. It is recognising the moment a job has become a tool, and knowing you can now build that tool yourself. The next lesson takes the objectives page from idea to something running.

title: What Lovable is and when to use it

content_blocks.text: In Lovable you build by describing. That makes the first sentence you write matter more than any button you press, so a few minutes spent scoping pays off fast.

You met Lovable in the previous lesson as the tool for turning a described idea into a working web app. This lesson walks you through doing it once, end to end, with a small real task: a lending tracker for your team library, the shelf of books and kit that people borrow and keep forgetting to return.
Pick a task worth building

Choose something small, real, and yours. The lending tracker works well as a first build because you already know exactly how it should behave: someone picks an item, records who took it and when, and the list shows what is currently out. You do not need anyone else to sign off, and you will know within a minute whether the result is right. That fast, personal feedback loop is what makes it a good first build, whether or not you manage a team.
Scope it before you type
Lovable builds roughly what you describe, so decide the shape of version one first. Keep it to what the tracker genuinely needs on day one, and hold everything else back.

cards.body: A list of items, each with a title, a type such as book or device, and a status of available or out.
cards.title: What it holds

cards.body: Borrow and return: record who took an item, then mark it back in later.
cards.title: The main action

cards.body: Your team, on a shared link. No logins for a first version.
cards.title: Who uses it

cards.body: Reminders, overdue chasing, and reports can wait. Keep version one small.
cards.title: What to leave out

content_blocks.text: Describe your first version

Open Lovable and start a new project. In the prompt box, describe the app in plain language, working straight from your scope above. There is no code to write and no database to choose. You are telling Lovable what the app is for and how it should behave, and it builds from there. Writing a clear prompt is a skill the general track already covered, so here you are just applying it to a build.

A description for the tracker might read: build a lending tracker for a team library. Show a list of items, each with a title, a type of book or device, and a status of available or out. Let someone borrow an item by entering their name, which marks it out and records the date. Let anyone mark an item as returned.
Watch it come together

Lovable generates a first version and shows it in a live preview. This is the moment the tool is built around: you describe, and something runnable appears. Click through it the way a colleague would. Add an item, borrow it, and mark it returned.
Verify it does the job

Test against your scope, not against how polished it looks. Run the one path that matters: can you borrow an item and watch it change to out, then return it and watch it change back? Check the smaller things against your scope note too, such as whether the type field offers book and device. If the model produced something plausible but wrong, you will only catch it by trying the real path, because a confident-looking screen is no proof that it works.

Before you share the link, check what happens to your data. A first generated version may reset when the page reloads, or may save entries somewhere everyone with the link can read. Confirm where entries are stored and who can reach the app before you put any real names into it.
Reflect

Notice where the app did something you did not ask for, or missed something you assumed it would know. That gap between your description and what appeared is the raw material for the next lesson, where you refine the app by describing the changes you want. Keep your scope note as well. It is the checklist that tells you when version one is actually done, rather than when it merely looks finished.

title: Building your first app

content_blocks.text:
Your first version of the app exists. It runs, it roughly does the job, and now you can see everything about it that is not quite right: a field in the wrong place, a list that should be filterable, a layout that looks fine on your laptop and breaks on a phone. Iterating is how you close that gap. In Lovable you do it the same way you built the first version, by describing what you want in the chat panel, except now each request is a small correction rather than the whole app.

You already know the describe, check, refine loop from the general track. This lesson is about how that loop behaves inside Lovable specifically, where every request you type can regenerate part of a working app you would rather not break.

The tool-specific catch: a broad instruction gets a broad rewrite. Ask Lovable to "make the signup page better" and you cannot predict what it changes. Ask it to "add a dropdown to filter events by city, above the event list" and you can check exactly one thing afterwards.
Change one thing at a time

The habit that makes iteration manageable is scoping each request to a single change. Type one clear instruction, let the app rebuild, then look at the preview before you type the next one. This is slower than listing five fixes in one message, and it is worth it: when something goes wrong, you know which request caused it, because only one thing changed.

Take the event-signup app from the previous lesson. You have a running list of events and a signup form. You want three improvements: a filter by city, a fix for the title that wraps badly on a phone, and a confirmation message after someone signs up. Resist the urge to ask for all three at once. Do the filter, check it, then move on.
Describe the change, and where it goes
When you request a change, say what you want and where it belongs. Lovable is editing a real interface, so location matters as much as behaviour.

cards.body: Add a dropdown above the event list that filters events by city.
cards.title: Add a feature

cards.body: After someone submits the signup form, show a confirmation message instead of reloading the page.
cards.title: Change behaviour

cards.body: On narrow screens the event title overlaps the date. Stack them vertically below a certain width.
cards.title: Fix layout

cards.body: Change the form heading from Register to Reserve your place.
cards.title: Adjust content

content_blocks.text: Notice that each of these names a specific element and what it should do. That is the tool mechanic. How to write a clear instruction in general is covered in the general track; here the point is simply to keep each Lovable request narrow and anchored to a part of the screen you can point at.
When a change makes it worse

Sometimes a request does the wrong thing, or fixes one part and breaks another. This is normal, and it is why you change one thing at a time. Lovable keeps a history of versions as you go, so a bad change is not permanent. You can go back to the version before your last request and try describing it differently.

Do not keep piling new instructions on top of a broken state, hoping the next one will sort it out. That tends to compound the mess. When a change goes wrong, revert to the last good version first, then re-describe the change more precisely.

If a request half-worked, it is often better to revert and rephrase than to patch the patch. "The filter appeared but it is below the list, move it above" is a fine follow-up. But if the whole page has scrambled, going back a step is faster than talking the tool out of a state it should never have entered.
Fixing layout and mobile issues

Layout problems are the ones you are most likely to miss, because you build on a wide screen and the break only shows on a narrow one. In the event-signup app, the event title and date might sit side by side comfortably on a laptop and then collide on a phone.

Check the app at a narrow width. Lovable shows a live preview, and there is usually a way to view it at a phone-sized width or open it on your actual phone. When you find a problem, describe it in terms of what should happen at that size: "on narrow screens, stack the title above the date instead of side by side". Describing the symptom and the screen size gives the tool something concrete to correct.

Verify visually, do not assume. A fluent "Done, the layout is now responsive" in the chat is not proof. Look at the preview at the width where it was breaking. This is the same reason you check any AI output: confident wording is not evidence that it worked.
Knowing when to stop

Iteration ends when the app is usable, not when it is perfect. Before each new request, ask whether the thing you are about to change would actually stop someone using the app, or whether it is polish you can leave. For an internal event-signup tool, "people can find their event, filter it, and sign up without the page looking broken on a phone" is usually the finish line.

A practical way to converge: keep a short list of what still bothers you, fix the ones that block use, and consciously decide to stop on the rest. The loop can run forever if you let it. Deciding it is good enough is part of the skill, whether you are shipping this to a team or just using it yourself.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can take a rough first app and steer it toward something usable: scoping each request to one change, saying where on the screen it belongs, reverting when a change goes wrong, and checking the result at the size where it matters. The next lesson takes this loop further, using it to build a real app from a description end to end.

title: Iterating on your app

content_blocks.text: You have already watched Lovable respond to your descriptions and reshape an app as you talk to it. This lesson names what you were doing and turns it into a repeatable method. You will build one real app end to end, from a plain description to something you could put in front of people, by directing a machine that writes the code for you.
What vibe coding is

Vibe coding is building real, working software by describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI write the code. The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025, and it captures something new: someone with no coding background can go from an idea to a working app in an afternoon, without touching syntax.

The roles are worth stating plainly. You describe the intent, the model writes the implementation, and you check whether it did what you meant. You are the product owner and the tester. The model is the developer. You do not need to understand every line it produces. You need to understand what the app is supposed to do and whether it does it.

Vibe coding is not AI doing everything. It is you staying in charge while the model handles the code. The moment you stop steering and just accept whatever appears, you have stopped vibe coding and started gambling.

For a manager, this is the real payoff: you can validate an idea yourself before you ask anyone to build it properly. It is also a foothold if you have no team at all. A recurring manual task that ends in a file or a form can often become a small tool you direct into existence in an hour.
Pick a task worth building

The build for this lesson is a conference session-feedback collector: a short form an attendee fills in after a session, plus a simple way to read what came back. It is a good candidate for a reason. The scope is small, the group of users is defined, and if it has a rough edge nobody is harmed. Anyone who runs a workshop, a training session, or an internal talk has this exact need, so it is a real job rather than a toy.

Not everything belongs here. A quick internal tool with a handful of users and low stakes is the sweet spot. Something that will handle sensitive data, serve hundreds of people, or need to keep running for years is a different kind of project, and pushing a described-in-an-afternoon build into that role creates problems someone else has to clean up. Keep your first builds firmly in the small-and-internal zone.
Scope before you describe

Here is the specific challenge of vibe coding, the one that separates a clean build from a frustrating one. The model is quick to start typing. If your description is vague, it will fill every gap with a reasonable guess, and reasonable guesses are often wrong for your situation. By the time you notice, the app is built on the wrong assumption.

So the work happens before the first prompt. You do not need diagrams. You need to answer four questions about the thing you are building.

cards.body: The inputs a person gives. For the collector: the session name, a rating out of five, and a written comment. Name these first so the model does not invent its own fields.
cards.title: What goes in

cards.body: The result you want back. Here it is a saved response and a simple view of average ratings and comments you can read at a glance.
cards.title: What comes out

cards.body: The steps in the middle. A person submits the form, the app stores the response, and it shows a confirmation. Each step is something the model has to get right.
cards.title: What happens between

cards.body: The edge cases. Someone submits an empty form, or sends the same rating twice. Decide now what should happen, or the model will decide for you.
cards.title: What could go wrong

content_blocks.text: Ten minutes answering these gives you a brief. That brief is the thing you describe to Lovable, and it is worth keeping in a note so you can refer back to it and stay consistent as the build grows.

The most common vibe coding mistake is describing a feature you have not scoped. "Add a way to see the results" gives the model nothing to aim at. "Show a page listing every comment with the average rating at the top" gives it a target you can actually check against.
Describe the first version

Do not describe the whole app at once. Build the smallest version that does the one thing that matters, confirm it works, then add the rest. This is the minimum viable product idea applied to a build: get the core flow right before you polish anything.

For the collector, the core flow is submit a response and store it. Your first description to Lovable might be:

Build a simple web app for collecting feedback after a conference session. Show a form with the session name, a rating from one to five, and a comment box. When someone submits, save the response and show a short thank-you message.

Lovable builds a working version and shows it in the preview. Once that flow holds up, you layer on the next piece as its own request: a results view that lists the comments and shows the average rating. After that, perhaps a way to choose which session the feedback is for. One request, one thing to check, every time.

This rhythm is what keeps a build recoverable. When you add a feature and something breaks, you know which change caused it, because you only made one. A single giant prompt that produces a tangle gives you no such handle.
Check it does what you meant

A preview that looks right is not proof that it works. This is the same reason you learned to verify any AI output in the general track: fluency is not evidence. A confident-looking app can still do the wrong thing.

So test it as a real attendee would. Open the preview, fill in the form, and submit. Did the thank-you message appear? Now try the edge case you scoped: submit an empty form and see whether it behaves the way you decided it should. Check the results view against what you actually entered. You are not reading the code. You are driving the app and comparing what it does to the brief you wrote.

When something is off, describe the gap, do not just say "fix it". "The rating saved as text instead of a number, so the average is wrong" points the model straight at the problem. Vague reports get vague fixes.

Making those responses persist for real attendees, and getting the app to a shareable link, is its own step. The next lesson covers it: deploying, sharing, and connecting your app to data. For now, verify the behaviour and shape in the preview.
What you can now do

You can take a real, small need and turn it into a working app by describing it, scoping before you build, and checking each step against what you meant. That is the whole method, and it is the same one whether you are collecting session feedback or sorting a folder of files.

The judgment matters more than the speed. Knowing what to build, scoping it clearly, and staying honest about when a job has outgrown a described-in-an-afternoon tool is what makes this a skill rather than a party trick.

title: Vibecoding, build a real app by describing it

content_blocks.text: From working preview to a live link

In the last lesson you built the feedback collector by describing it, and it ran in the preview. The preview is only visible to you inside the editor. To let anyone else open it, you publish the app, which gives it a real web address you can share. This lesson walks through publishing, sharing that link, and connecting the app to a store so the responses people submit are actually kept.

Publishing and saving data are two separate steps. A published app can look finished and still be throwing away every response, because a form needs somewhere to write to before it keeps anything. Do the data connection before you send the link out.
Step 1: Publish the app

Open your project in Lovable and use the publish control in the editor. Publishing builds the current version of your app and puts it on a public web address. The first time, you will get a default address provided by Lovable; you can attach your own custom domain later if you need the link to sit under your organisation.

Give it a moment to build. When it finishes, you have a live URL that loads the same app you saw in the preview, now reachable by anyone who has the link.

A published Lovable link is public to anyone who opens it. There is no sign-in wall unless you build one. Do not use a plain published form to collect anything sensitive, and assume the address can be forwarded on.
Step 2: Connect a place to keep the responses

A form on its own does not remember anything. When someone submits the feedback collector, that response has to be written somewhere, or it is gone the moment the page closes. Lovable connects to a hosted data store for exactly this, so your app can save each submission as a row and you can read them back later.

In the editor, open the data or backend integration option and connect a data store. You will be asked to authorise the connection and, for the feedback collector, to have a table that holds each response: who submitted it, the rating or comment, and the time it came in. Once the app is wired to that table, every submission from the live link lands there as a new record.

Describe the data step the same way you described the app. A prompt like "save each submitted response to the connected database and show me a confirmation message" lets Lovable wire the form to the table for you, rather than you configuring it by hand.
Step 3: Verify before you share

This is the step people skip, and it is the one that saves you. Open the live URL yourself, in a private browser window so you are not signed in as the builder, and submit a test response the way an attendee would. Then check that the response actually appears in your connected data store.

If the submission shows up as a new row, the whole chain works: live link, form, and storage. If it does not, the form is not connected to the table yet, and you have caught it before anyone real hit a dead form.

content_blocks.text: Step 4: Share the link

Now send the URL to your attendees. Because it is a normal web address, you can drop it into an email, a calendar invite, a chat message, or a QR code on a slide. Anyone who opens it gets the current published version.

One thing to know about updates: changes you make in the editor do not go live until you publish again. You can keep editing safely, because attendees stay on the last published version until you push a new one. When you are happy with a change, publish again and the same link updates for everyone.
Republishing reuses the same address, so a link you have already shared keeps working after an update. You do not need to send a new URL each time you change the app.
If you are an individual contributor

None of this needs a team or a budget. If you are the one running a workshop, a retro, or a sign-up sheet, you can publish a small collector, connect it to a store, and have real responses arriving in minutes, without filing a ticket or waiting on a platform team. The verify step is where you earn trust in it: once you have watched your own test response land in the table, you can send the link out knowing it holds.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can take an app from a private preview to a live link, give it somewhere to keep the data people send, confirm the whole chain works, and share it. That is the full loop for a builder-tool app: describe, build, publish, connect, verify, share. From here, the same steps scale from a one-off feedback collector to any small tool your team keeps asking for.

title: Deploying, sharing, and connecting your app to data

content_blocks.text: Every team space in Confluence grows the same way. Someone creates it for a project, pages pile up, meeting notes and decisions and half-written specs accumulate, and a few months later nobody can tell you what state the work is actually in without reading twenty pages. The AI features in Confluence are aimed at that problem. They sit on top of the pages you already have and help you find them, summarise them, and draft against them, so what your team wrote down stays findable and usable.

The exact name keeps moving. Atlassian has been folding these capabilities into Rovo and Atlassian Intelligence, so the label in your instance may differ from a colleague's. What matters is the behaviour described here, not the wording on the button.
It reads your space, not the open web

The thing that makes these features useful is where they look. A general chatbot answers from its training. The AI in Confluence answers from your content: the pages, spaces, and comments you already have permission to see. This is the grounding idea you met in the general track, applied to a knowledge base. When you ask for a summary of a project space, you get a summary of your project, not a plausible-sounding guess about projects in general.

That also sets the boundary. If something was never written down, or lives in a space you cannot open, the AI cannot see it either. It works with the knowledge your team captured.

content_blocks.text: The example worth holding onto

Picture a project space that has been running for two quarters. Forty-odd pages, several contributors, decisions scattered across meeting notes and comment threads. Your steering group does not read any of it. They want to know where things stand.

This is the job these features are built for. You point the AI at the space and ask for a short status digest: what has shipped, what is blocked, what changed since last month. Instead of one person spending an afternoon reading and rewriting, you get a first draft of that digest in a paragraph or two, pulled from the pages themselves. You still read it and fix it, but now you are editing a draft rather than starting from a blank page and a wall of notes.

content_blocks.text: The next lesson shows how you trigger each of these. For now the point is the pattern. Every one of these jobs is the AI reading what your team wrote and handing you a head start from material that already exists.
What it does not do

Grounding on your own pages makes the output more trustworthy than a generic chatbot. It does not make it correct. The AI can still misread a table, miss a caveat in a comment, or report a blocker as resolved when the page saying so is out of date. Confident wording is not evidence the summary is right, for the same reason you learned in the general track.

So the digest is a draft you sign off, never a fact you forward unread. The next lesson pairs each feature with that safe-use habit.

You do not need to own a space to get value here. If you maintain a single runbook or one team page, the same features help you keep it current and let a colleague get the gist without reading all of it.

Treat AI-generated summaries as unverified until you check them against the source pages. A summary that reads cleanly can still carry a wrong date or a dropped dependency, and it now looks authoritative.

title: What Confluence AI does

content_blocks.text: You met what Confluence's AI features are for in the last lesson. This one is hands-on: how to actually run a search, summarise a long page, and draft a new one, using a single real task as the thread. Say you have just come out of a project kickoff, you need to write up the notes, and you half-remember there is an onboarding runbook buried somewhere in the space but you cannot recall where anyone filed it.

The AI features may appear under Atlassian's own branding (Rovo or Atlassian Intelligence) rather than the word "AI", and exactly where each control sits depends on your plan and your admin's settings. Look for an AI or sparkle icon near the search bar or in the editor toolbar. If you cannot see it at all, it has most likely not been switched on for your instance yet, which is a matter of admin configuration rather than a fault at your end.
Search: finding the buried runbook

Ordinary Confluence search matches keywords. The AI-assisted search lets you ask in plain language, so instead of guessing the exact title someone gave the runbook, you can type what you actually want: "where is the new-hire onboarding runbook for the delivery team". It reads across the pages you have access to and returns a direct answer with links to the source pages, rather than a raw list you then have to sift.

Two habits make this reliable. Name the team or space if you know it, because it narrows the field. And always open the linked source page before you act on the answer, because the summary is a pointer to the truth, not the truth itself.
Summarise: getting the gist without reading it all

Once you have the runbook open, or any long page, use the summarise action to get its shape before you read every line. On a single page the control usually sits near the top of the page or in the AI panel. You ask for a summary, and it returns the key points, which is enough to decide whether this is the right document and which section you need.

The more useful move is summarising across several pages at once, for example asking for the current state of a project that spans a dozen pages. That is powerful, and it is also where the one real risk of these features lives.

A cross-page summary is built from pages you already have permission to see. Confluence will not surface anything from a page or a space you cannot open yourself, so a summary cannot leak restricted content the way the raw idea of "reading across pages" might suggest. The real risk is different: a summary strips away each page's own context, so a stale figure, a superseded decision, or a dropped caveat can end up sitting in one confident paragraph with nothing to flag that it has gone out of date. Before you paste an AI summary somewhere wider, such as an open page or a chat, check the claims that carry weight against the source pages, not just whether the content is shareable.

content_blocks.text: Draft: writing the meeting-notes page

Now write the notes up. Create a new page and use the draft or AI writing action in the editor. Give it the raw material, such as your rough bullet points from the kickoff, and tell it what you want, for example "turn these into a structured meeting-notes page with decisions, owners, and next steps". It returns a formatted draft directly in the editor that you can then edit like any other content.

Treat the draft as a first pass, never the final page. The AI does not know who actually owns an action unless you told it, and it will happily write a confident, tidy sentence around a detail it invented. You are the one who was in the room, so the facts, the names, and the decisions are yours to confirm.

content_blocks.text: The one rule that ties all three together

Every one of these features can be wrong while sounding completely sure of itself, for the same reason you covered in the general track: fluency is not evidence. So the workflow is the same each time. Let the AI do the fetching, condensing, or drafting, then verify against the source before you rely on it. That is the difference between the tool saving you time and the tool quietly introducing a mistake into a page other people will trust.
